subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL ASSENT TO LEGISLATION CREATING BRITISH CARIBBEAN FEDERATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL ASSENT TO LEGISLATION CREATING BRITISH CARIBBEAN FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today Her Majesty the Queen is giving royal assent to United Kingdom legislation enabling the creation of a British Caribbean federation. The federation will not legally come into being until a constitution is adopted and a governor general appointed. Nevertheless, the passage of the Caribbean federation bill is such an important milestone that in those colonies which will eventually comprise the federation, that is to say, Jamaica, Trinidad, the Leeward islands, the Windward islands and Barbados, today is being celebrated as Federation day.
I am sure all hon. members will wish to join with me in expressing, on behalf of the people of Canada, our gratification at the substantial achievement represented by the legislation which is being submitted for royal assent today, and our warmest wishes for the future of the federation.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL ASSENT TO LEGISLATION CREATING BRITISH CARIBBEAN FEDERATION
speechtext: I know that every hon. member of this house, and I am sure every Canadian, welcomes this historic milestone. I think there is one reason why all of us must feel a sense of the historic significance of what is taking place, and that is the fact that it was from the area of the Caribbean that the first reported knowledge of the new world was brought back to Europe. Christopher Columbus discovered what became known as America first of all by a visit to the Caribbean. Therefore today we are seeing the fulfilment of a great historic event, and I know that every one of us here will wish to the new federation success, happiness, prosperity and a great future within the commonwealth of free nations which we all respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I took
notice of a question by the hon. member for

Inquiries of the Ministry Lambton West as to the action being taken by the Department of National Revenue in the light of the announcement of the United States government's policy of subsidizing exports of cotton. Section 6 of the Customs Tariff provides for the application of dumping duty on imported goods of a class or kind produced in Canada where the selling price to the purchaser in Canada is less than the fair market value as sold for home consumption in the country of export. On July 25 instructions were issued to all collectors of customs requiring them to alert their appraisers to the present situation and to require extra vigilance with respect to imports of these commodities. I shall now read the instructions and place them on the table. They are as follows:
Value for Duty Cotton Textiles
For some time, there has been a two-price system in the United States for raw cotton. Manufacturers in that country have been required to pay a price for their supplies of raw cotton that was approximately 6 cents per pound higher than the price at which similar cotton was sold for export.
Beginning August 1, 1956, United States exporters of yarns, fabrics and manufactured articles made from cotton will be eligible to claim an equalization payment from their government based upon the estimated amount of cotton used in the manufacture of the goods and the difference between the United States domestic price and the export price of raw cotton.
This arrangement could enable exporters to sell their products to Canada at prices below the fair market value obtaining on sales in their home market. It will, therefore, be necessary for appraisers to exercise extra vigilance. All entries of goods from the United States containing cotton are to be taken subject to amendment and careful attention is to be given to ensure that invoice descriptions are adequate and certified fair market values are in compliance with the law.
In respect to any importations where the appraiser considers investigation by the department is warranted, a copy of the invoice and, where possible, a sample of the goods are to be promptly forwarded to the department. Samples of fabrics should not be less than 12 square inches in area and should be large enough that the pattern may be identified. In each instance, where invoices are submitted, the importer should be advised that the value is being inquired into and amendment of the entry and any subsequent entries of similar goods may be required at a later date.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is the minister now prepared to answer the questions asked by the hon. member for Lambton West on Tuesday and Wednesday, of this week with respect to diversion of the waters of lake Michigan? fMr. McCann.]

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; I have the answer here in reply to both those questions.
A bill providing for temporary diversion of an additional 1,000 cubic feet per second of water from lake Michigan to the Illinois waterway for experimental purposes for the aid of navigation and for a period of three years was passed by the United States congress in Washington in the session which just recently ended. The President, however, according to our information, has not yet taken any action with regard to signing that bill or vetoing it.
By the definition in the boundary waters treaty of 1909, lake Michigan is not a boundary water. It does, however, come within the scope of the treaty because article II makes specific reference to "all waters which in their natural channel would flow across the boundary or into boundary waters", as is the case with lake Michigan. The interpretation of article II is a rather complicated matter and I think it would not be very useful for me to go into it now. It was, however, discussed at some length in the standing committee on external affairs in 1955. It appears that the proposed diversion of the waters of lake Michigan would not come under the jurisdiction of the international joint commission unless it was referred specifically to it.
The Canadian government expressed its views to the United States government on the proposed additional diversion in a note dated February 13, 1956, which was tabled in the house on March 8. In this note Canada took the attitude that the enactment of the proposed legislation would be prejudicial to the navigation and power interests of both countries. By doing so we have already expressed our concern with regard to it.
In so far as the other question was concerned regarding the Long Lac-Ogoki diversion, I should point out that Canada consulted the United States concerning this diversion into lake Superior, because the effect of this diversion was to increase the total amount of water at Niagara, and Canada wished to receive due credit for that increase in the arrangements for the division of water at Niagara for power purposes. This being a diversion into boundary waters and not out of boundary waters, it did not require agreement between the two countries under the boundary waters treaty, though a special agreement was reached and embodied in the Niagara treaty of 1950.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 31 the hon. member for Selkirk asked the following question:
When Peter Thom, treaty Indian, was admitted to Fisher River reserve hospital, was a third-year medical student the only person available to treat him?
This Indian was admitted to the Altona, Manitoba, hospital on July 1 following injuries he had received across the border. At the request of the doctor in charge at Altona he was transferred by ambulance to St. Boniface hospital the same day. He was treated there for dislocation of both hips and placed in a plaster cast. His condition improved, and on July 13 St. Boniface hospital authorities asked the regional office of the Indian health services if he could be transferred to an Indian hospital. A bed was available in the Fisher River Indian hospital and he was transferred that day to this hospital.
Inquiries of the Ministry
The doctor in charge at the Fisher River hospital had resigned and his replacement had not yet arrived, and his assistant, a third-year medical student employed for the summer, was at the hospital. This medical student had instructions to call a practising physician 20 miles distant for assistance at any time, and it was this physician who was the designated physician in charge at the hospital and available when required.

subtopic: FISHER RIVER RESERVE HOSPITAL-STATEMENT ON QUALITY OF TREATMENT

supplementary question. Why was this treaty Indian, Peter Thom, moved to Fisher River hospital when no doctor was due there for three or four days? I should like to know this, also. At the inquest was it established whether the Indian, Peter Thom, was run over intentionally or accidentally?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: FISHER RIVER RESERVE HOSPITAL-STATEMENT ON QUALITY OF TREATMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume the authorities at St. Boniface hospital felt that this man was in a suitable physical condition for transfer to the Fisher River hospital. subtopic: FISHER RIVER RESERVE HOSPITAL-STATEMENT ON QUALITY OF TREATMENT
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration whether he will look into it? The man died in this hospital.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: FISHER RIVER RESERVE HOSPITAL-STATEMENT ON QUALITY OF TREATMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have looked into the matter. The regional supervisor in Manitoba drew this case to the attention of the attorney general of Manitoba and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have investigated it; but since this accident or crime, or whatever it may have been, took place in the United States, in the state of North Dakota, the only thing the attorney general was able to do was to draw the proceedings at the inquest to the attention of the state authorities in North Dakota. I am informed that is being done and that the police are keeping their file open.
Of course, it is not the duty of my department, or indeed of the federal government, to enforce the law in the province of Manitoba, and much less in the state of North Dakota; but because this man was an Indian we did follow the matter up with the appropriate provincial authorities.

The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration regards extravagance as a very light matter. In this he is far out of contact with the experience of the average *Canadian taxpayer. The exemptions allowed to Canadian taxpayers are quite inadequate; [DOT]and if the minister would exercise his ingenuity to eliminate extravagance it might be possible for the Minister of Finance- I think it is possible now-but it might bring the Minister of Finance to make these exemptions adequate, to raise them beyond the present inadequate figures of $1,000 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons without dependents.
There was a point raised about mirrors, and the question was asked in the committee about the price of two eighteenth century mirrors, that were purchased for the embassy. The first information we had from the department is shown at page 390 of the report, where the official said:
I am told that it was approximately $2,000 for "those mirrors.
Later on the price of the mirrors was inquired into further by the department and the answer was brought back to the committee at page 433 that the two mirrors did not cost $2,000 but cost $1,078.
I have read these details to bring to the attention of the house the rather impressive items which lurk behind some of the big rfigures that appear in these estimates. It
Supply-External Affairs seems to me that we are too disposed in this committee to take these items in the aggregate without going back into the details behind them. When we go back into the details, this is the sort of thing that unfortunately we find there.
As I said last night, we cannot now undo this extravagance. This expenditure has been incurred, but I bring it to the attention of the house in order that the house may warn the government and the Department of External Affairs that it does not intend to tolerate extravagance on this scale in the future.
There is, however, one thing we can do in reference to this year's estimates in this respect. We are dealing with item No. 95, which provides approximately $2,000,000 for construction, acquisition or improvement of buildings, works, land, equipment and furnishings. In this item, as we see in the details at page 178 and following, there are specific amounts set out for capital as well as operational expenditures at various embassies and diplomatic posts abroad. There is one subitem at the end, at the bottom of page 183, to which I invite the attention of the house. After listing in detail the proposed expenditures on operations of a capital nature at all these posts abroad, there is one item headed "Miscellaneous- unallotted capital items"-$805,000.
The facts I have brought to the attention of the house in connection with the embassy at Rio ought to alert the house to the necessity of exercising as much supervision over proposed expenditures by this department in this respect as may be possible, but here we are told that there is in this item a sum of $805,000 that has no tag whatever attached to it and which, if it is passed, the department is at complete liberty to expend in the purchase or improvement of any property or the purchase of furnishings anywhere in the world. There are no strings attached to it.
I submit to this house, as I submitted to the standing committee on external affairs, that this is not the way in which the House of Commons ought to do its business. One of our duties here is to assert the principle of strict parliamentary control over expenditures, and here we are told, on the face of these estimates, that there is a sum of $805,000 that is not earmarked for any place in the world and which can be used for the purpose of a capital outlay by the department anywhere in the whole globe.
I submit that is not a proper way for the House of Commons to deal with proposed expenditure. I moved in the committee that the subitem should be stricken out, because while we are quite prepared to deal on its

Supply-External Affairs merits with any proposed expenditure for which a case is made out, nevertheless we do not believe in just providing money loosely after this fashion for the government to use in any way it sees fit. I am glad to say that in the committee my amendment came very close to passing. It was defeated by a vote of only nine to six. It was supported by all Conservative and C.C.F. members of the committee although, of course, it was opposed by the Liberal members, and they were supported by the Social Credit member on that committee.
Mr. Chairman, I am going to renew that motion now, and I hope that what I have said about the extravagance in connection with the purchase of the embassy at Rio and its furnishings will alert the house to the danger of placing large sums of money like this at the disposal of the department without any strings attached to them. It is difficult enough in the case of these expenditures that are made abroad, where it is only very rarely that a member of the committee or a member of the house has an opportunity of seeing with his own eyes the results, without placing a sum of nearly $1 million at the disposal of the department without any strings attached to it save that it must be expended abroad on capital account for buildings or furnishings.
The excuse given by the department is that they may have the opportunity of making a good buy somewhere, that there are capitals in the world where the department wishes to acquire property for the housing of its diplomatic representatives and if opportunities present themselves they should be in a position to take advantage of them. I think that is a very dangerous doctrine to follow. That doctrine, if followed, could result in a very serious weakening of parliamentary control over expenditures. We are sitting here now seven months a year, or perhaps even more, and we have estimates and supplementary estimates introduced about four times a year. I cannot see that any lengthy period is ever likely to elapse before parliament would be in a position to deal with any opportunity that is offered.
The principle of parliamentary control over public expenditure is a very important principle and we should not be parties to weakening it. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That item 95 of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs be reduced by the sum of $805,000 by elimination of the "unallotted capital items" on page 183.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter was, of course, discussed in detail in the committee on external affairs, and I am glad it was. The hon. member has also discussed it in

detail last night and this morning, and I certainly have no quarrel with that because I am just as interested in the avoidance of extravagance in the expenditure of Canadian funds as he is. The hon. member knows, of course, because he has been a guest and I am sure a very welcome guest at a good many of our missions abroad, that an embassy or a legation is not a private residence. It is the official residence of the representative of Canada, and when we buy property naturally we try to keep that in mind. It is Canada in that particular foreign capital and we want that property, that residence, to be suitable. We also want it to be permanent. In the case of Rio, for instance, we hope that this embassy will be the official centre of Canada in Brazil for 50, 75 or maybe 100 years, and so we purchase for a long time.
In purchasing we look for something suitable, a house for the job and not for any particular person. That means that an embassy, which is not a private residence, has to have accommodation for official receptions, official dinners and all those things which are an important part of diplomatic activities especially, if I may so, in a South American state. There is nothing in our mind-and I mention this because the hon. member referred to it two or three times-of keeping up with the Joneses. That does not seem to me to be a very pertinent observation in any event, because whether one wants to keep up with the Joneses in any activity would depend very largely on where the Joneses are and where they are going. Very often we should be well behind the Joneses and possibly at times we should be well ahead of them.
So far as Rio is concerned, in this capital we are not concerned with aping the customs and the habits of the diplomatic representation of any other country. We do what we think is right for Canada. If we had wished to keep up with the Joneses in Rio, some of the Joneses have spent between a million and a million and a half dollars on their embassies in that capital. We buy buildings when we are able to buy them with economy as well as efficiency, and with representational propriety in mind. So far as Rio is concerned, it is a great metropolitan capital of an important South American state, the South American state with which we in Canada probably have our most important commercial' and political relationships, and I say that without implying any reflection upon our relations with any other South American state. But it is possibly true that our commercial contacts with Rio are more important than those with any other South American country.

It is also true that Rio is one of the most expensive capitals in the world, and that has a bearing on the purchase of property there. In other places where it is not so expensive we get property much more cheaply, and that does not mean that we attach less importance to our representation in those capitals or more importance to our representation in Rio. It just happens that in those capitals, some of which are comparable to Ottawa in real estate and residential values, we are able to purchase residences for our representatives at $42,000 in one place, $85,000 in another, $44,000 in another, $56,000 in another and $73,000 in another. Those residences for those sums of money are suitable for Canadian representation there and we do not pay any more if we do not have to.
As for Rio, there is obviously an advantage in trying to buy property there rather than renting, if we can do so. We have been renting a property in Rio for 14 years, and if my hon. friend could see some of the rental figures and compare them with rental figures in Rio generally he would realize that this is not an economic or effective way of doing business there. During that time we have turned down places for purchasing because they were too expensive, and we have been offered residences there which were less expensive but which were entirely unsuitable.
My hon. friend referred to the fact that we had an option to purchase Mr. MacCrim-mon's residence there at $80,000. The fact of that particular matter is that two or three years ago we offered the owner of this house $190,000 for that residence and were turned down. We made that offer even though our ambassador on the spot said that in his opinion it was not suitable for a Canadian embassy in Rio. However, after further investigation we thought it was suitable and we offered $190,000 and were refused. Meanwhile we were paying a very high rental. In this last year we were told that we would have to vacate the house we were renting at a figure of something over $2,000 a month, and the owner of a very good residential property in Rio came back to us with an offer which was about $250,000 less than he had made to us a few years before.
Having regard to all the circumstances and after an independent valuation by, I think, three real estate dealers, and as the alternative was renting another house at a figure comparable with the rental we were paying, we decided this was a satisfactory purchase. If we had rented another house we would have had to pay a rental which included all the taxes on the property and other charges. When we purchase diplomatic property we get diplomatic exemption from these taxes
Supply-External Affairs and these charges, and that fact normally makes it desirable to buy. The furnishings of the embassy have been gone into in detail. This house was not furnished by the man who happened to be ambassador at the time. It was done by somebody brought from Canada, an independent interior decorator.
More important, possibly, is the question which is the subject of this amendment, that we should not have in our estimates a sum of money-the figure is $800,000-for the purchase of properties abroad without specifying how much we want for each property in each country. We would be limited in this way to the purchase of properties within that amount in any country.
I submit that this would be an uneconomic procedure, and I make that suggestion for two reasons. One is that we in this department are still in a period of expansion. I hope we are reaching the limit of our expansion, though we are continually approached by other governments and indeed we receive suggestions in this house that we should expand our diplomatic representation. When the period of expansion is over we will have satisfied our residential property requirements and we will not need more houses for that purpose. But we need them now. We need to have accommodation in five or six capitals, and we may need more if we have to open more offices.
There are times during the course of the year when we are offered property which is satisfactory and economic for the job to be done. Sometimes those offers are kept open only for a few weeks, because in some of these capitals it is extremely difficult indeed to get property. If we had to specify our purchases in advance, one of two things would happen. We would only put in the amount we were absolutely certain of spending because we had agreed on valuations for properties which we know we would need during the course of the year. Or we would put in for each capital where we needed property an estimated amount, and at the end of the year we might find that as offers had not been forthcoming at prices we could pay we would have been able to spend only one-third or one-fourth of that amount. Hence we would have either inflated estimates on the one hand or we would have to miss economic opportunities to purchase on the other.
That is why we in our department have considered it good business to put in this lump sum, so we can take advantage of opportunities during the year when we know there are certain places where we want to buy property if we can get suitable property.
It is not correct, Mr. Chairman, to say there are no strings attached to this amount.

Supply-External Affairs Whenever a suitable property is available and it is felt by the department to be suitable on representational as well as business grounds, treasury board has to agree to purchase after a very careful examination and valuation of the property. Of course we in the department cannot spend any of these sums of money without treasury board approval and without an exhaustive survey by the board. It is therefore my opinion that this amendment, far from leading to economy, might have the effect either of the inflation of our estimates to take advantage of any opportunities that might arise, or might lead in the other direction, namely that of extravagance; because we might not be able to take advantage of good offers during the year. With property values going up in these capitals, in common with property values in Ottawa, if we did not have the money to buy a property on the spot, next year we might have to pay 50 per cent more for something else.

Mr. Chairman, there is one question I should like to ask the minister, in view of his statement, and it is this. When the national gallery purchased some pictures which cost a great deal of money-I believe about $800,000-from the Prince of Liechtenstein last year, they did not have the money on hand with which to do it. However, the deal was made and then the sum was put in the supplementary estimates. That seemed to be the policy of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, or rather the policy of the minister under whose jurisdiction the national gallery comes. What would be the objection to using that same method in the Department of External Affairs?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There would be no objection, Mr. Chairman, if it could be done in connection with property purchases. But our experience has been that the owners of property that we consider suitable to purchase are not willing to hold the property for us until we can get an estimate passed by parliament at the next session. We feel that if it were not done in the way in which we are proposing to have it done, we would lose these properties.
We have taken this matter up with treasury board in order to see whether there is some way in which we could work out interim financing, so we would be able to have the exact amount later in the estimates to confirm the interim financing. We are still discussing the matter with them, but so far treasury board has not come up with any solution which appears to be any more effective or economical than the one we are proposing.

Realizing the difficulties that are inherent in the present dispersal of this department amongst several buildings and the resultant difficulty of providing for

So we have taken our place on the list of priorities. 99. Grant to the United Nations association in Canada, $11,000.

Is the minister making any progress in discussions with the United Nations association on the possibility of having better public information services in Canada in connection with the work of FAO, WHO and UNESCO?
I raise this question each year when the estimates come up and also discuss it with the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but apparently no department of government in Canada seems to worry a great deal about making known to our people in Canada the problems that are being faced by these international organizations.
I noticed that in the Toronto papers yesterday a great deal of publicity was given to a swimming star, but rarely do we see anything in the Canadian papers regarding the very imaginative work which is being undertaken by some Canadians in different parts of the world.
The last Colombo plan release I had gave information that some 40 Canadians are in different parts of the world. It is on a typewritten sheet, but there is no information about their names, where they are or what they are doing. It would seem to me that some of these people come from Halifax, Regina, Calgary or Vancouver, and some of the people in the cities where these young people live should be given some information from time to time regarding their work. I think it is going to be increasingly difficult to get additional funds for these agencies that must have additional funds if the taxpayers of Canada are not given more information from time to time.
About a year ago the minister mentioned that probably a United Nations organization would be the organization-it would not be the responsibility of government-that should be given this responsibility. If they are

given that responsibility then more funds should be made available. Can the minister make some comment as to whether any discussion has taken place with a view to increasing the grant, or whether his own department feel they should set up an agency? I realize that criticisms have come from the Progressive Conservative party from time to time regarding what is being done with respect to new expenses, but I feel that here is one important sector of the work of external affairs that should have additional funds.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I know that my hon. friend has a very special interest in this matter, because we have discussed it, and I know that for some time now he has not been satisfied with what is being done in this respect, both in the government and possibly outside the government, through grants of this kind. All I can say is that in our information division we have not been allotted appropriations which would enable us to do more than we are doing in publicizing the activities of international organizations and the Colombo plan in Canada.
But I would point out to him the grant we make to the United Nations association to assist it in this work, and I think the more of this work that can be done by voluntary organizations the better. This particular grant has helped the United Nations association do a good deal of publicizing of the activities of the United Nations and its specialized agencies. For instance, the association prepares and distributes the world review of United Nations activities for Canadian schools, and about 52,000 copies are printed monthly, which are distributed by the provincial departments of education. I also know that the Colombo plan organization has increased its information activities through its central office fund in the last year; but I am not going to quarrel with the suggestion of the hon. member that more could be done, and I am not going to quarrel with him that more should be done. In fact, the resources we have now do not permit us to do any more.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this amount covers, as my hon. friend knows, the graduate fellowships and scholarships which are granted to Canadian students from federal funds for study abroad. As he also knows, the scholars in question are chosen not by the government but by the Royal Society, which administers these schemes.
In 1955-56 the Royal Society allotted 16 scholarships, 12 fellowships and 28 other awards. These awards are given for study abroad not only in the natural sciences but in the social sciences. As my hon. friend knows, the money was originally paid out of blocked funds in European countries which accrued after the war, but that source of assistance has come to, or is coming to, an end. It is hoped that we can continue this assistance to scholars through a regular appropriation of this kind, not from blocked funds.
I agree that possibly there has not been as much publicity given to this as is desirable, but the Royal Society of Canada has from time to time issued pamphlets to universities where the information is available. The most recent one I have before me was issued just a few weeks ago, which gives a good deal of information as to how to apply, the qualifications required and the nature and scope of the assistance. This should supply all the information that is required by any applicant for a scholarship, and I am informed that it is given quite wide distribution by the Royal Society.

Mr. Chairman, when the day comes that blocked funds are used up and we shall appropriate money in this parliament specifically for this purpose, would it be the intention of the government to see that scholars and students are able to go to countries other than those mentioned in this vote?

105.	To provide for the Canadian government's contribution to the United Nations expanded program for technical assistance to under-developed countries in an amount of $1,800,000 U.S., notwithstanding that payment may exceed or fall short of the equivalent in Canadian dollars, estimated as of December, 1955, which is, $1,798,875.

Mr. Chairman, this item is to provide for the Canadian government's contribution to the United Nations' expanded program for technical assistance to underdeveloped countries. This matter was given considerable attention in the committee, and it is not my intention to make any extended remarks on this item. I am sure we all appreciate the work that is being done in this connection.
I was somewhat perturbed to come across an article in my home town newspaper, the Abbotsford, Sumas and Matsqui News for Wednesday, June 27. The heading of this article is "Critical of Assistance Given Asiatic Countries" and it has to do with both the technical assistance programs and the Colombo plan. I want to read just two or three paragraphs from this article and perhaps the minister would like to take notice of the contents. The first paragraph is as follows:
That the technical assistance agencies attempting to raise the standards in industries in Asiatic countries are failing in the task for which they were designed, is the personal opinion of Dr. John W. A. Brant, physiologist, who is currently vacationing with relatives in Abbotsford.
The third paragraph from the top in the article reads as follows:
His work during the past year was similar to his year in Ceylon with a team of United Nations technical officers.
I am just picking out pertinent paragraphs. Further down in the article the following appears:
Dr. Brant suggests the technical programs are far-fetched. They are not in step with the culture and historical progress of the country. Dr. Brant explains that United Nations technical experts and experts from other similar agencies, when they are sent to the Asiatic countries, are assigned to government branches or commercial and academic institutions. Quite often those who are trained turn their knowledge to personal gain, rather than passing it on to the masses.
Another paragraph is as follows:
In many instances, the technical assistance being given is causing more harm than good. In effect, the present programs are attempting to force 1,000 years of progress on these countries overnight.


A final paragraph reads:
Of the three agencies, Colombo plan, United Nations, and the United States, which are currently supplying assistance to Asiatic countries, the Colombo plan is the most effective, Dr. Brant believes.
I do not know just how qualified this gentleman is to make these observations, but certainly if he has been a member of the teams in these various countries his words should be worth something. I thought possibly the minister might be interested in making some inquiries regarding this gentleman, learning by what authority Dr. Brant speaks and whether or not his observations are correct.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do that, Mr. Chairman. I know, of course, there have been some criticisms made of the technical assistance programs. It would be surprising if that were not the case, because there are great difficulties in the provision of technical assistance in these countries. So often it is not possible to get enough of the best technicians to do the work. That is one of the reasons I wish we could have some kind of international civil service organized under the United Nations, so people would be continuously available for this kind of thing. Having regard to these difficulties, I nevertheless think the project itself has been effective and successful although, as I have said, it has had its disappointments.
I hope the committee will feel this expenditure of $1,800,000 is very worth while. In some ways the Colombo plan-and we are not talking about that-has been more successful than the United Nations technical assistance program because of the intimate relationship between the member countries, which has made it easier to develop cooperative projects; but the United Nations scheme which is now under good organization and administration-the head is a Canadian- is doing a very worth-while job. I shall be glad to look into the particular matter raised by the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if it might not be possible to do something under our own civil service in this regard. We know there is a great shortage of competent personnel to assist countries whom we would wish to assist in a technical way. Would it not be possible to open up a new sort of career for Canadians, both men and women, who would be interested in devoting their lives to this very significant form of aid to those who are less fortunate than we are? In other words, is the department considering at all giving some sort of moral support to universities in the training of young men and women who would be prepared to enter this new concept of civil

service, nomadic perhaps in a certain way, whereby they would be on tap, as it were, to be sent to different countries when requests come from them.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know our own civil service commission has tried to help whenever it could in the provision of experts of this kind for the United Nations, but I realize that my hon. friend would go further than that. I should tell him that this very matter is now under active consideration at the economic and social council meeting now being held in Geneva. This is a matter in which our delegation is very interested, and the secretary general of the United Nations is also very interested in it. I hope that in the course of time something will be developed along these lines on an international basis.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately there are many committees sitting which makes it impossible for one to be here when one wishes. The hon. member for Fraser Valley indicated in his address on the first item that I would take part in this debate. I rather hoped to deal quite extensively with the United Nations, but I see that we have reached the technical assistance stage, so I will have to try to confine my remarks to the particular item we are discussing.
I am thinking now of the question that was dealt with to some extent in the United Nations. That is the matter of SUNFED, the special United Nations fund for economic development. I found in the discussion, which interested me a great deal, the suggestion made by a great many of these countries who would take part in it that in the operation of the fund those who were the contributors would not be in a position to regulate the use of the fund. I know there is a great deal of argument in favour of that course, though I would personally prefer to see those who are contributing in some way have a greater say in the actual expenditure.
Earlier in this debate the hon. member for Prince Albert quoted a statement to the effect that every dollar put into investment in this field is worth $5 in defence. Possibly he is quite right, but I would say we should only invest to the degree that the investment can be absorbed in the particular country that is being given assistance. I think that is one of the problems we have to deal with specifically.
We find that the countries of southeast Asia are generally considered to be neutral. I do not know what a definition of neutrality would be, unless it could be that a decision would be reached by that country as to whom they might think would be the victors in
Supply-External Affairs the event of a catastrophe and on that basis they would decide on the country of which they would be in favour. Be that as it may, that is the only field from which we are going to be able to draw any reserve in the event of war or a similar catastrophe; therefore I think we should do everything within our power to see to it that we assist these people in every way possible.
I am satisfied that if the United States today is being held in some disregard by these countries-or for that matter, if we ourselves are being held in disregard by them- the reason is that they feel every time they receive financial assistance of any kind certain strings are attached to it. For that reason we have to revise our thinking on technical matters.
Asians, I believe, fear it. They have just got over a long period of colonialism, over 300 hundred years of it, and they do not want to have any more of it. I have listened with a great deal of interest on former occasions to speeches in this house having to do with United States investment in this country. We find in this country and in this house a great number of people who are completely opposed to further United States investment in this country because, they say, there are strings attached to it. We might only place ourselves in the same position in Asia in some of these underdeveloped countries, and we come back to the same conclusion that these people reach in this country. They are no more desirous of that help than we are, because they feel there are certain strings attached.
Therefore, as I said earlier, I think we should revise our thinking to a degree on this particular problem. I wonder whether the government has given any thought to a different approach to the question. We have the field of technical education and university training, authority for which is given to the provinces alone. I would propose, though, that instead of just continually giving aid to the underdeveloped countries we change our thinking and possibly develop in Canada an international university and technical training school, to which Canadians would not be allowed to go, perhaps centralized in one of the prairie provinces because of the facilities we have there, agricultural and otherwise. We could invite students from India and some of the other underdeveloped countries to come to this college or school, whichever you call it, for the purpose of training them in our field of agriculture, in irrigation methods and any other things we feel it necessary that they must know before they are able to utilize the machinery and equipment we send them.

I am satisfied that our provinces would not take exception to this, because we would not be entering into their field of education. We would be doing something for the world in an effort to stimulate an interest in those underdeveloped countries in becoming more familiar with our techniques of operation. I am satisfied that the U-S.S.R. is doing something along similar lines. The over-all effect might be that coming into contact with Canadians as they are bound to do, they would appreciate more of the problems that we have, for indeed we have certain areas of our country that are underdeveloped in the way of capital investment by this government. However, instead of continually putting more and more dollars into a field of investment which is not appreciated because of the strings attached, I think we should find some new approach that would be acceptable to these former colonial countries.

Before the item carries I wish to discuss a matter which I intended to discuss the other day. I have been greatly intrigued by the "package deal" that the Minister of National Health and Welfare endeavoured to negotiate in relation to the United Nations last fall. On July 26 I asked the minister if he would be here during this discussion, and he said he would be; but yesterday he gave me to understand that he is prevented from being in Ottawa because of an unfortunate accident to one of his children, which detains him at home.
X wonder whether I might ask of the Secretary of State for External Affairs the questions that I desired to ask of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, if he does not feel that that would be imposing on him? If he would be willing to answer the questions or give his idea as to what the Minister of National Health and Welfare would have said, then I should like to talk about that matter for a little while.
I am interested not only in the fact that there was a "package deal" which this house


did not know was going to come up. There was no announcement whatever about it, and as far as we know the government knew nothing about it. If people, with no more permission from this house to go and speak for it respecting international affairs than, as far as I know, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has, are able to go to the United Nations and commit Canada by implication as that minister did last year, I do not know what outrageous things we might expect to be sprung on us at almost any time. I feel that under the circumstances a matter so serious as that should never have been taken up until we had a chance to discuss it. Perhaps I am quite wrong; I just want to be advised in the matter.
I had several questions which I desired to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Probably I would be well advised to read those questions first so the minister will have a chance to give them some thought.
First, will the minister give the house an account of his attempt in November and December, 1955, to obtain the admission of 18 nations into the United Nations general assembly in the so-called "package deal" which he supported?
Second, what in a general way did the minister conceive to be the advantage to be derived from the admission of this "package" to the United Nations general assembly?
Third, why were these particular nations chosen?
Fourth, name in order the nations on the list, and in the case of each give the special reason for including that particular nation on the list.
Fifth, where was that list made up-in Ottawa, in New York, in Moscow-or was it the result of the collaboration of all three?
Sixth, it was reported that when a United Nations person asked the minister what was the reason for Canada's stand to admit all 18 of these nations, including Mongolia and other communist countries, the minister said, "Our interest in the matter is government policy." Did the minister say those words?
Now I think I have something on which the Secretary of State for External Affairs can go to work, if he so desires; but while his experts are going into this matter, which probably is quite a surprise to them, may I say just a word or two about this question of Outer Mongolia? This matter of attempting to get Outer Mongolia into the United Nations brings up the whole question of the recognition of red China and the whole question of Chiang Kai-shek, the Chinese nationalist government, and their right to be recognized as the government of China and to be in their position in the United Nations.

It probably is not generally known that Outer Mongolia never did belong to Russia except during the years 1912 and 1913, when it belonged to czarist Russia for a little while. Mongolia, Manchuria and Sinkiang formed a belt of territories or possessions along the northern border of China. They had been Chinese possessions since the days of Genghis Khan, if I am correctly informed. Consequently these three provinces were under the control of the Manchus, and when the Man-chus were disposed of as the result of the work of Dr. Sun Yat-sen and Chiang Kai-shek, naturally the ownership of these three territories would come into the hands of Chiang Kai-shek and nationalist China. There can be no doubt about that.
Russia did nothing sufficient herself to get control of these three provinces although she had been trying to do so for a long long time, even before the days of the communists. Why should Outer Mongolia, which, as far as rights are concerned, still belongs to nationalist China and Chiang Kai-shek, be made into an independent nation, "a liberated nation" I suppose, according to modern terminology used by the communists, the pro-communists and the communist dupes? Why should a nation like that be admitted as a member of the United Nations general assembly? That is a question that will require a lot of answering and a lot of explaining. I should like to have the minister say a word or two on that matter. Perhaps his experts are not prepared to do so. If they are not, I shall read a statement which will indicate-

North Atlantic Treaty Organization-[DOT]
107.	To provide, subject to the approval of the governor in council and notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, for special administrative expenses, including payment of remuneration, in connection with the assignment by the Canadian government of Canadians to the international staff of the North Atlantic treaty organization (part recoverable from the North Atlantic treaty organization), $35,484.

Last year it was my privilege to be in attendance at NATO with a group of parliamentarians from this country. As a matter of fact it was just about a year ago now. The session had been called for the purpose of seeing what could be done to implement the economic aspects of NATO. I was very pleased indeed that the Secretary of State for External Affairs saw at the time of the drafting of the charter a need for this particular clause, for it becomes more and more apparent as time goes on that NATO itself would be dying more quickly or would be dead if it were not for the hope that there would be some greater binding force than the military aspect that we have at the present time.
I know there are certain newspapers or certain groups that take a dim view of parliamentarians making these annual excursions. I might say this, however, Mr. Chairman. Aside from the matter of fellowship, which was irrelevant and unimportant, I certainly obtained a greater degree of understanding of the problems that are facing our European friends and other members of NATO in this regard. While it is true that some of us can speak from time to time on questions pertaining to our own country, when it comes to this matter of international problems it is necessary that we be somewhat more familiar with them than we are at the present time if we are actually to understand what are the problems that face these member nations.
The only way in which that can be done, so far as I can see, is to take a group of parliamentarians to Europe-and I would say a different group each year-in order that they might become more familiar with those questions and might come back with some intelligent reasons for what they think should be done to assist our cause.
In my discussions with these friends I found that it was the fear of war that was responsible for the bringing into existence of NATO. But fear is not a binding force, in my estimation, and we want a binding force. I would therefore say that the other aspect which the Secretary of State for External Affairs emphasized when he was on the committee drafting the charter is the more important one, and that it should be emphasized more and more. It is up to us as members of this house to try to give him ideas. As one of the three wise men I am sure he would be anxious to hear how we would implement the economic factor, for in that way alone lies the continuance of NATO.
The world today is divided into several blocs. We have the Arab bloc, the Soviet

bloc, the China bloc, the Southeast Asia bloc, and the American bloc, as it is sometimes called. In trying to analyse these problems as we see them, we can arrive at a reasonable solution only by integrating ourselves, by becoming more closely associated more particularly with the nations which we have reason to believe are our friends and allies, and by co-operating with them. General Gruenther, who is to leave the association, has certainly gained the respect of everybody. However, I am satisfied that his successor will prove to be just as able and capable as he was.
We were particularly well represented. We were very fortunate I might say, in our own organization in having with us-he has now been transferred to the head office-Air Vice Marshal Campbell and Brigadier Anderson, who are doing a noble work. Indeed, I am satisfied that it is only as a direct result of the fine work that Brigadier Anderson has done among our troops in Soest that we have today men and women who have become ambassadors at large in Europe, following the unfortunate incidents when the Canadian troops first came over and settled in that area. It was only through his work, his integration, his ability to sell the fact that Canadians are human beings just the same as other people, that they were made so acceptable to the German people. I am sure we cannot compliment this man too highly for the work he has done and for the high regard in which he is held by Europeans, particularly by the Germans in the community with which he is associated.
There is, however, one other factor that interested me. When I was at the United Nations last year I was privileged to be in attendance at a special meeting that was called by some of the original signatories to the North Atlantic treaty. Senator Robertson was the guest speaker, and at that meeting were representatives from each of the NATO countries. I believe the only country which was not represented on that occasion was Turkey. Each one of us was privileged to give a five-minute address following the senator's remarks. The feature that stuck with me most was the statement by every last representative from those countries that NATO would die unless the economic aspect was brought forward and developed.
This suggestion is very definitely borne out by the action of Iceland. There just the military aspect has been emphasized at all times; we have sacrificed the economic aspect. I would say that we must develop that aspect in order that we may re-establish ourselves as a North Atlantic Treaty Organization that will continue to function in order to offset the forward march with which the Soviets
Supply-External Affairs are plaguing us today. NATO can be, and in the future should be, developed more and more in the economic field.
I see that it is just about one o'clock, Mr. Chairman. However, if the committee will bear with me for about two minutes, I shall have finished. I have only one or two observations to make with respect to methods.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that the hon. member has consent?
Agreed.

My reference is to methods of developing the economic end of NATO. They are only three in number, in fact. I would make the suggestion that while we have the three wise men, the organization might set up a special committee for the purpose of studying only the economic aspect of this matter. It would be more a committee to inquire into the possibilities of integrating trade between these nations.
First I would suggest an overseas investment program. There would be no giveaways as far as I am concerned, because of the strings attached on the basis I mentioned earlier in respect to the United Nations, but it would be just as applicable in NATO. This program would be administered through an advisory council in consultation with investors.
Then, in the matter of civil production, it would be most important to develop primary production for use and marketability; develop a nation in proportion to its adaptability, but at all times decentralize the organization so no part is solely dependent on the other. I think every nation wishes to keep its sovereignty and that it wants to seem independent even in this matter of trade, and not dependent solely on what someone else is producing. There should be a recognition of NATO by all members, they should recognize that they have a role to play either in economic or military matters, or both, to be protected at all times.

I think that points out one of the weaknesses of the NATO organization. There is no real meeting of minds between governments. I have a very high regard for the civil servants who are acting there on behalf of the governments, and particularly for the one who represents Canada. But if there is going to be reality in this subject of Atlantic unity there has to be what I call this meeting of minds, and it cannot come through meetings, no matter how frequent, of civil servants. It can only come through the meeting of ministers, those who really make policy.
What has happened all too frequently in the past is that arrangements have been arrived at, and properly so; then cabinet ministers have gone over and within a matter of a few hours have agreed to the arrangements which had hitherto, of course, been agreed upon. I do not think that is good enough. If we are going to make something out of NATO ministers must meet ministers, and problems must be threshed out in the council. I hope Canadian ministers will take a far greater interest in the work of NATO than they have in the past. I exempt the Secretary of State for External Affairs from that condemnation.

While the minister is dealing with that, perhaps he could tell the committee whether the government has in mind undertaking any negotiations with the United States concerning access from the western boundary of British Columbia through the panhandle of Alaska to salt water. As the minister knows, this panhandle drops down over that western boundary for about half the whole length of the western boundary of British Columbia. In recent years there have been extensive developments taking place in the mining field in that part of British Columbia. This is a question which will have to be handled quickly. It cannot be left indefinitely because of the developments that are taking place at the present time in that portion of the province. I wonder if the minister would deal with those two points this afternoon.
