speechtext: My estimates are coming up next.
But this is the item for the international joint commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I also have one.

While I am prepared to
co-operate, I do not want to be foreclosed by one minister saying, "You should have brought it up under the other's estimates".

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Bring it up and we shall see.

What I wish to ask is simply this. Is the Secretary of State for External Affairs prepared to discuss the present situation with regard to the Columbia river in so far as the international joint commission is concerned and the problems about which we both know, or would he himself

Supply-External Affairs prefer to leave the whole matter to be discussed on the estimates of the other department; because if we can have a better discussion there I would be prepared to defer it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think there would be a better discussion on the estimates of my hon. friend's department, because his department is making the preparations for these intergovernmental talks that are about to take place with which the international joint commission, the Canadian side, will be associated; therefore I think it would be more constructive if we could postpone it until his estimates come up, and they are coming up right after mine.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
110.	To provide for Canada's share of the expenses of studies, surveys and investigations of the international joint commission. $199,180.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to make a few remarks on this item. This morning I was pleased to hear the minister say that the proposed Passamaquoddy development had been referred to the international joint commission. The minister will recall that on May 7 I moved:
For a copy of all letters, telegrams, memoranda and other documents exchanged during the past three years between any department or officials of the federal government and the international joint commission, the government of the United States of America, and any other government or organization or individuals, relating to a survey or surveys of the economic feasibility of the development of the Passamaquoddy tidal power project.
I had a partial return from the department, and I had hoped for a full return before the minister's estimates came before the house. However, the minister said this morning, I think, that tomorrow at Washington there would be a joint statement-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Today.

I wish to thank the minister for sending me a copy of the reference, which I received just a few minutes before I came down to the house. It is too bad that this reference had not been made public earlier, so that a study could have been made of it while the minister's estimates were before the house. From a cursory study I notice that the reference to the commission authorizes them to determine the costs, to determine the effect on the economy of the United States and Canada of this development. They are given the advantages of the reports of 1950 and 1952. I also note that the United States government, subject to the availability of funds, is to incur costs of up to $3 million and the Canadian government up to $300,000.

It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that there is a great discrepancy in the amount Canada is contributing to this investigation as compared with that which is being contributed by the United States. It is ten to one. We in the maritime provinces are interested not only in the proportion of one to ten in this development, I can assure the minister. I wish to assure the government that is not the case. We feel that if this Passamaquoddy project is developed it should be more or less a fifty-fifty proposition, and any benefits which accrue from the development of the Passamaquoddy-I see the hon. member for Charlotte here and I am sure he will agree with me in this-should go to the United States and Canada, and the maritime provinces in particular, in equal proportions. There is no doubt as to the interest that exists in this project in the maritime provinces, because in the return I received from the minister there were recommendations from boards of trade of the county of Charlotte which the hon. member represents and from other boards of trade in the maritime provinces.
I do think, Mr. Chairman, our federal government was rather dogmatic in its reply to some of the representations made by the United States government with reference to this development. I am afraid there has been a very lukewarm attitude on the part of the federal government with regard to this development. This has been recognized not only by the people in the maritime provinces but also by people in the state of Maine. I had a letter from Senator Smith of Maine which I read here some time ago in which she said she was very much afraid that the Dominion of Canada was not taking the vital interest in this matter that the state of Maine was, and which she hoped the United States in general was taking.
I should like to quote from a memorandum sent by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to his excellency the ambassador of the United States. It is dated April 5, 1956. I quote from this memorandum:
The Canadian authorities concerned have given careful consideration to this matter-
That has reference to the international joint commission. I continue:
-and it is assumed that further discussions will take place concerning the specific terms of the reference which might be presented to the international joint commission. It also seems desirable to include in the joint reference provision for an investigation into the effect that the proposed tidal power project would have upon the fisheries in the area.
That is naturally very important, but it is not the only consideration which we in the

maritime provinces have in this proposed development. The memorandum goes on to say:
Having regard to the foregoing, the Canadian government is prepared, on the following conditions, to join with the United States government in a reference to the international joint commission on a survey of the proposed Passamaquoddy tidal power project:
(a)	It is proposed that each country assume responsibility for part of the required surveys and investigations. Canada would be responsible for the investigation into the effect the project might have upon the fisheries, and Canada would assume the cost of this investigation to an amount not exceeding $300,000.
I point out again, Mr. Chairman, this rather indicates that the main interest Canada has in the Passamaquoddy development is simply in connection with the fisheries. I continue:
(b)	Each country would facilitate the extension to it of the required surveys by agencies of the other country, as well as the entry of personnel and equipment, on the understanding that all information obtained in the various surveys would be made currently available to each country through the international joint commission.
(c)	In joining in the reference to the international joint commission, the Canadian government would make no commitment regarding the eventual construction of the project.
I hope this is not an indication that the Canadian government is not anxious to bear its full share of the Passamaquoddy development if it is found feasible and practical. We do not wish to see the United States achieve control and have the absolute use of the Passamaquoddy development, and we do not wish to see Canada having an interest only in protecting the fisheries of the bay of Fundy.
I understand, and I think it is general knowledge in the province of New Brunswick, that there are quite powerful fishery interests in that province that are more concerned over what might affect the fisheries in the bay of Fundy than they are over the great power project in that province. I also understand that from inquiries made in 1950 the fears of the fishermen in the bay of Fundy are rather unfounded, and there is no great danger to the fisheries there. However, this investigation will determine that. 1 also understand it will take three years in order to complete this investigation, and possibly we will not know what the attitude is going to be until the three-year period has elapsed.
I would like the minister to tell us this afternoon whether the federal government is as concerned about the development of Passamaquoddy as is the United States, and particularly the state of Maine, or whether we are interested only in protecting the fisheries in that area.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can assure my hon. friend that we are sincerely interested in both aspects of this investigation, the
67509-436J
Supply-External Affairs development of power and also the effect any such development might have on our fisheries there. We share the interest of the United States in this investigation, and we will share fully with them in the results of the investigation.
Financially?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We will share in every way in the results of the investigation. If this investigation shows it is economically feasible to proceed with this matter and we are satisfied to that effect, then naturally we will be happy to share with them in future developments. It has been felt, however* that the fisheries aspect of the matter is one in which we have a very special interest,, possibly a greater interest than our friends, on the other side of the line, and therefore we have taken a special responsibility in regard to that aspect of the investigation.
The cost of that part of the survey will be about $300,000. The United States will be putting up about $3 million in this investigation, but that does not mean the ratio of our interest or the ratio of our participation in the results of the investigation will not be 50-50. There have been technical experts on our side, I know, and my hon. friend knows this better than I do, who in the past have been sceptical about the economic feasibility of this development. It has already been investigated.
Some have been optimistic, I might say.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, some experts have been optimistic about this, possibly more on the other side of the line than on this side. However, the investigation is going to take place. We must all hope that as a result it will make possible a power development which will be economically advantageous to that part of Canada, and will not interfere with our very important fisheries industry.
I think there is nothing more I can add at the present time, Mr. Chairman. I am sorry this reference was not before my hon. friend prior to today. We have been doing our best to get the United States government to agree to a joint reference. We had ourselves agreed on terms some weeks ago. They have been considering it in Washington ever since, and we received their final agreement to this particular document only yesterday.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Terminable services-
111.	Colombo plan, $34,400,000.

I might say, Mr. Chairman, that the question of the Colombo plan was discussed in some detail in the committee

Supply-External Affairs and I shall not take the time of the house in repeating all the evidence that was produced there. However, I would like very briefly to indicate the point of view of a great many members of the committee, in fact I think I would be safe in saying practically all members of the committee.
There was a considerable interest in the Colombo plan revealed in the committee, probably a greater interest than in any other single item. Most of the members of the committee I listened to felt that the government would increase the appropriation for the Colombo plan in coming years. Mr. Nik Cavell, the witness who appeared before the committee, indicated that it was not always possible to spend all the money that could be spent because there were not always technicians readily available. In the light of what Mr. Cavell pointed out, there was some hope expressed that through the cooperation of industry and so on, if further moneys were advanced by the government ibr the Colombo plan we could obtain this technical assistance. In other words, the intimation was that if more money were advanced by the government in the coming years for the Colombo plan Mr. Cavell could certainly find the technical assistance to carry it out.
The question of the Colombo plan is something which is of great interest to the general public, at least that is the case in my part of Canada. During the last three or four months I have received 70 or 80 letters not only from individuals but from various organizations including missionary groups, the women's institute and various church groups as well, concerning the request I put forward in this house that the government should increase its annual appropriation for the Colombo plan. From what I have been able to learn many other hon. members have also received similar letters.
It is to be hoped that next year the government will see fit to increase this annual appropriation for the Colombo plan. We all know that the Soviet union and its satellites have apparently adopted a new method in their aim for world domination, and the new method, as all hon. members know, is the smiling war, the economic war, the handing out of promises of more assistance than we are giving to those parts of tiie world that have not taken sides as between the east and the west.
I think it is worth while on this point to note that since hundreds of millions of people in India, Pakistan, Indonesia and parts of Africa have just recently regained their political freedom, they are now very anxious to obtain their economic freedom as well.

It is probably quite truthful to say that most people in these countries have never had enough to eat at any time in their lives, and now when they have obtained their political freedom they see an opportunity for economic freedom so they will be able to get enough of the necessities of life. Naturally they will be very anxious to look to any country that promises such help, regardless of its political ideology.
The people to whom I have talked who have spent a considerable time in those countries and speak with some authority on the subject point out that people who have not enough to eat are not interested in political ideologies. I think that is something any hon. member could easily understand. They tend to look with favour on countries that promise them aid and so on. I know that in previous debates in this house various hon. members have shown the amount of aid the Soviet union is promising to these various so-called underdeveloped countries, and an article in one of the principal newspapers of Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia, which pointed out that aid under the Colombo plan was a mere pittance by comparison. Of course the Soviet union apparently has not delivered much of the aid it has promised these various countries, but there is little doubt that it could, if it wished, deliver a good deal, particularly in the form of technical assistance and machinery, since it has been pointed out in this debate and many times in this house before that the Soviet union is no longer a land with an ox-cart economy.
Bearing all this in mind, and particularly in view of the great interest in this country in the Colombo plan, the government should see fit to increase the appropriation in another year. If nothing else, it is a matter of self-defence. Apparently the Soviet union is going all out in an attempt to gain the minds of the so-called underdeveloped countries and, if you will pardon me for coining a phrase, it is entering the mind by means of the stomach, so to speak. Unless we want to see all the sympathies of the people of these countries slip away from us, it is in our interest to increase aid to them.
There is one other matter I wish to mention in this regard, and that is the question of training people from underdeveloped countries to help themselves. All hon. members know, I think, that many students from Pakistan, India and so on have come to this country and obtained training of one sort or another. I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned this morning that he thought it was a very good idea for the students to actually work, if necessary, in our factories, farms and so on.

I should just like to say that I have had some experience of that in my constituency. We had nine students from Pakistan who were there under the Colombo plan. They were learning about farm machinery at the Massey Harris Ferguson plant in my city, and they were there for about six months. They lived in homes throughout the community. They took part in all the social activities of the community. They played badminton, took part in little theatre activities, spoke at the service clubs and so on. They were invited out socially at all times and everybody, if I may say so, treated them very hospitably and, I might even go so far as to say, made a fuss over them. This treatment was genuine and from the heart, and I am quite sure it would be the same in any community or small city in this country.
After those people went back to Pakistan I received letters from them, as did many other people in Woodstock. The impression that was created in their minds as to the merit of our way of life is something those people will never forget and will carry with them always. Now that they have gone back to Pakistan they will hold positions of considerable importance in the country, and they cannot help having a very great influence on the thinking of the people with whom they associate. I have no doubt that the administrators of the Colombo plan will continue to carry this out. I think it is something that can be carried out and expanded, because I can think of no better way of selling our way of life to people in the eastern countries.

During the past year or two, very often the Soviet union has been either threatening or promising-I am not sure which it is-to indulge in large-scale schemes of assistance to underprivileged countries. I am not sure that their performances have matched up with their promises, but we would be making a very serious error, as has been pointed out before, if we in the west tried to enter into some form of competition with the Soviet union in the giving away of forms of assistance. The most productive way of stopping this rivalry, of course, is through the United Nations. If the Soviet union is really serious about improving the lot of the underprivileged people of the world, and if we are really serious about improving their lot, then let us together help them through the only international agency which really can do it; that is, the United Nations.
I see no reason why Canada cannot do far more than we have in the past to make the special United Nations fund for economic aid a reality. If we want to avert this competition in give-aways with the Soviet union, we
Supply-External Affairs can only do it through the United Nations, and we in Canada have to do far more than we have in the past through that agency.
I, too, would like to see the funds allotted to the Colombo plan increased, as would all my colleagues. But, important as the Colombo plan is, I do not think we ought to forget that, taking the over-all picture, the assistance which can be given by the United Nations in the long run would be more important. I have always opposed unilateral programs of giving money and assistance to other nations, because no matter how generously it is done or how genuinely it is done, there nevertheless rests in the minds of the recipients a certain fear that the donor has perhaps some ulterior motive. However, if we were trying to help the underprivileged people collectively through the United Nations, then I am sure that fear would disappear.
Yesterday the minister told us that the increase in the funds allotted to the Colombo plan was very substantial. There is an absolute increase of $8 million, which even these days is substantial, an absolute increase of some 32 per cent. But when one breaks it down into the per capita contribution by the people of Canada, what does it amount to? In our supreme generosity, from the fund of wealth we have in this country-and next year when there is an election we shall be told how well off we are-we are only giving away another 5 cents per capita per month. That is what $8 million amounts to. I am convinced that were there any will in this government to do better, they could do so, because they would have the support of the people of Canada. Time after time I have said in this house that the Colombo plan has caught the imagination of the people in a way much more obvious than, of course, has NATO.
I say we could make a much more substantial increase, and I am convinced it could be used productively. The minister yesterday reminded us that we could advance money to our friends under the Colombo scheme and it could be wasted. That I grant. But we can also waste money in this country just as easily and just as expeditiously. However, I doubt very much whether there would be the waste which perhaps some fear.
Let us take the case of India alone, and what applies to India of course applies to other nations. Within the next five years the Indian government intends to invest some $10 billion in capital goods in that country. I do not think for a moment that the Indian government has that amount of money behind it, either in its own treasury or in the savings of the people. Then how is it going to finance this great scheme of

Supply-External Affairs industrialization, which is only another five-year plan, another instalment of a general plan? Either India has to get more generous help-I am not talking about gifts but about loans at low rates of interest-from the more fortunate nations of the world, or India is going to print paper money, and the result of course will be devastating inflation with all the social consequences which will ensue.
I am quite sure that India and the other Asian nations who are partners of ours in the Colombo plan could very productively use much more money than we are prepared to give. We also ought to remember this fact, which a recent United Nations economic survey has pointed out. We industrial nations find that our standard of living is constantly rising, but the nations which are the primary producers of the world, the nations of Asia, find that their standard of living is constantly falling, so that as the years go by there is a greater disparity between the industrial nations who have much of the riches of the earth and these people in Asia who have not. We can afford to give much more than we have given, and I am convinced that the people of Canada would like to see it done.
But there is another aspect of the Colombo plan or of any other plan such as this. This, after all, is a plan to assist other nations, aid from government to government. I am not yet convinced that is always the best way of achieving the end we have in view, and I am certain that the end we do have in view is that of improving the lot of the less fortunate people in this world. Just a few months ago a brief was presented to the Gordon economic commission by the United Church of Canada, of which I happen to be a member, and if I am critical of that body then I am inferentially critical of myself. But this brief said in part:
Empty stomachs do not linger over the dissertations on the advantages of democracy. They go where food is and make friends with those who can provide it, without too much regard for political theories. If communism outwits and outruns the western world in feeding the hungry, we will have only ourselves to blame.
That is true. The United Church brief asks the government to do very much more than is covered by these estimates, and I am convinced that the government should have done very much more. But there is something else which the people of Canada can do. I believe the government of Canada ought to give the lead, but I think the people of Canada as responsible citizens ought to ask themselves, what can we do as individuals? I remind the committee of a scheme started in Norway two or three years ago, when the people of Norway collected money amongst

themselves to give to the less privileged people, a gift from people to people. A gift from people to people is a much more significant thing than a gift from government to government.
The other year I put a proposition before the congregation to which I belong, which happens to be a fairly well off, middle class congregation of about 1,500 people. I suggested that we might all perhaps give the sum of $1 each, no more and no less, not somebody giving $10 and nine others giving nothing, but that each of us might give $1 each as a gift to less fortunate people in another part of the world, a gift obviously without strings attached, a gift without any connotation other than that we felt a sense of brotherhood and a sense of responsibility for those who were not as well favoured as were we. I received the most inestimable assistance from Mr. Escott Reid, our high commissioner in India. I wrote telling him what the plan was and asked him if he could find in the area of New Delhi a village of perhaps some thousand souls who might be able to use productively as a gift from Canadian people the sum of $1,000.
Mr. Reid went to great pains and great trouble. He located a village, sent me photographs of it and gave me a breakdown of the social characteristics of the village. I thought for a while that I had sold my colleagues in my congregation on an idea which I considered worth putting into practice. Unfortunately I was wrong. The matter came before the governing board of the congregation and they took the position that this was the responsibility of government. I think that was an abdication of citizenship. We cannot pass everything to government. Individuals themselves must take some responsibility, and I suggest to the officers of the United Church that they approach their own congregations and see if we as individuals in Canada cannot build up a scheme whereby in our own small way we will do something to show the people of Asia that in our own well-being we have not forgotten them.
Two Canadians did do something about it, and I believe the minister knows of this case. A couple of Canadians who live in British Columbia, Dr. and Mrs. Naranjan Grewall, went to India two years ago. Dr. Grewall happens to be a native of the Punjab. He had come to this country as a young man, worked hard, arduously and successfully, and he took his Canadian wife back to the area where he was born. He saw once again the poverty from which he himself had fled. He saw the need of the people in that community. He saw children who had no building in which they could be taught.

There was no school of any sort whatsoever. He said right then and there, "I am prepared to build you a school. I have gone to Canada and have been lucky. That is now the land of my adoption. I should like to share some of my wealth with you in the land of my birth." He built a school for the people of his native village.
A little later his wife, Mrs. Grewall, offered to build a hospital, and it is now being built. The school was opened by one of the officials in the office of the high commissioner. There, I think, is a very practical example of citizenship at its best, the sort of citizenship that realizes that out of our own wealth, out of our own well-being, we must give some part to help those who are less fortunate and less well favoured.
This does not in any way mean that the government can abdicate responsibility for giving leadership, but I do think the people of Canada, if they were given the proper lead, would be ready to play a much more significant part in helping others by way of gifts from people to people.

Mr. Chairman, I do not hesitate to congratulate the minister on increasing our gift to the Colombo plan by $8 million. I think that has been endorsed by all Canadians. But, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to get on the band wagon and say that we should give another $10 million or $20 million'. I do not forget that the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of the C.C.F. and others-and I agree thoroughly with them in their position have said that there should be an increase in the pensions of civil servants who are not getting enough to keep them living. I can give as examples some cases where they do not get two meals a day. I know the good book says that charity begins at home. I say it begins at home here with respect to the civil servants who have spent their lives in the service. I think of one man especially. He was a mail carrier. He is getting $85 a month, and he is keeping a wife who is ill. I think those civil servants have the first call. I am not going to vote for any increased contribution to the Colombo plan until these civil servants are taken care of.

I want to join with the
other hon. members who have spoken in support of the increase in the assistance to the Colombo plan this year. I do so because I feel that it is one of the most positive aspects of our Canadian foreign policy. It seems to point in the direction of the new diplomacy of economic assistance. Canada has come through various stages of assistance to underdeveloped countries since the war.
Supply-External Affairs After the war Canada took part in aid to Europe, which was largely based on the need for reconstruction in war-devastated areas. Then indirectly through the Marshall plan we rode on' the United States coat tails in further assistance to Europe. Today I feel that in the Colombo plan, in the program of mutual aid and technical assistance, we are pointing in the direction of an objective in the field of external affairs that is greatly to be desired, namely the time when we shall be able to match our program of military assistance with a program of technical and capital assistance.
The reason I wanted to say just a word at this time, Mr. Chairman, is that I feel that in the Colombo program we are making a real contribution to the moral aspects of the problem of international relations. It is a program that is carried out largely within the framework of the commonwealth. I have always felt that Canada's position as a member of the commonwealth of nations places her in a very favourable role so far as international affairs are concerned. But during a short stay at the United Nations last fall I was very much impressed to find that actually it is Canada's position as a commonwealth nation that gives us a role in world affairs, as one of the middle powers, far exceeding in importance that which our numerical and economic strength would otherwise justify. I think this commonwealth Colombo plan is evidence of the excellent contribution we can make in this regard.
The commonwealth is one of the few positive moral forces in world affairs today. We had the Earl of Home speak to us recently, and I was impressed as he gave us his interpretation of the new role of the commonwealth in world affairs. He referred to it as a positive moral force. He referred to it as a community of nations which is actually operating in that respect in this day when we are depending upon an atomic stalemate to give us a rather uneasy peace or, in the phrase often used by the minister, to establish a balance of terror. It is an encouraging aspect of Canada's foreign policy that we are able in this way to make a positive contribution to the role of Canada in world affairs. It is one that we trust we shall be able to increase as the years go by, as the immediate military emergency declines and as we are able to move into the more positive external affairs policy of providing economic assistance rather than military assistance on a large scale.
On this point, Mr. Chairman, there is just one question that I should like to present to the minister. In making personal contacts in the UN with members of the delegations

Supply-External Affairs from the southeast Asia countries, especially the members of parliament from those countries, I found that they had an extremely warm attitude toward Canada. We are not suspect in any way as a colonial power. Our background is absolutely beyond suspicion in that regard. We thus have a tremendous advantage in promoting the program of the west in that very important arena of world affairs.
However, I had pointed out to me by several of these representatives the fact that very little literature presenting the western viewpoint is available in cheap form. It would appear that the U.S.S.R. is making available all sorts of penny pamphlets telling of all the marvellous things the Soviet is doing or is intending to do in this new phase of foreign policy, of economic and technical assistance. These pamphlets are made available at a nominal sum to the millions of people in these Asiatic countries, and they are read avidly. They are mainly political tracts.
On the other hand, these people who have been in touch with the situation point out that there is available very little cheap literature presenting our side of the story. The only books they saw that would be within the price range of the ordinary people in those countries were our cheap paper-back novels. I am wondering whether that is a legitimate observation, and whether the Department of External Affairs has any interest in this particular problem.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words on this particular point. There are a great many things that I should like to have said on the minister's estimates, but some of us were tangled up with the labour estimates. At this stage of the session it is necessary to figure out where one is needed most. I figured that my main concern was at home, so I stayed with the Minister of Labour. I knew, of course, how well our interests in this department were being looked after by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-
The hon. member for Winnipeg North.

Yes; I mean the hon. member for Winnipeg North. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is so prominent around here that everybody forgets that there is any other Winnipeg member.
The particular matter under discussion, namely the Colombo plan, is something that I believe we should think about a little bit more. I am not concerned about the amount of money, provided it is spent in the right manner and provided that the people who are

contributing it are getting some credit for doing so. I might say that I have always taken the position, and I always will, that the United Nations was set up for the purpose of handling all the problems of rehabilitation after the war and the maintenance of peace. That organization has within it all the machinery to take care of all the problems that we are attempting to sort out on a regional basis. Because we are getting away from the United Nations, in my judgment it not only weakens the United Nations but it will make for a lot of duplication and waste in the money that is appropriated for such purposes as economic aid under NATO or the Colombo plan which have separate administrations.
I am not so sure whether the ordinary people who are the recipients of such aid under the Colombo plan are getting the full benefit of it or whether the countries contributing are getting any credit for it. The history of aid for the last 15 years, at least in countries such as China and Egypt and others, has been that it has not paid off by way of friendships. The governments presently in power in those countries which need economic aid take the money and distribute it for their own purposes, so very little is made known to the people as to the country that was the source of the relief.
My main point in making that statement is this. If you take a look at the United Nations set-up you will find that, starting with the general assembly, the security council, the trustee council and those small bodies, which with their secretariat run the show, built around that organization there are committees and commissions designed to take care of every problem connected with rehabilitation and maintenance. I do not believe the scheme of taking pieces out of the U.N. and setting up duplicate organizations in every part of the world is going to strengthen the U.N. in the final analysis. In my judgment, the future peace of the world will hinge upon the proper operation of the United Nations as such. For example, if it is desired to distribute food to any part of the world, there is an adequate organization connected with the United Nations to take care of it, the world food organization. When it comes to building up and taking care of the children of the world, there is also a committee of the United Nations functioning for that purpose.
As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris said a moment ago, the Soviet union makes a lot of promises on paper. Canada and the other countries of the commonwealth contribute a great deal towards that children's fund through the United Nations. I have

seen a lot of films and a few magazine articles on this subject, but I have never yet seen a film in which there was one Canadian shown. It is always United States nurses, doctors and technicians. No other country has received any credit in any of the films or articles that I have seen, except the United States. Now, perhaps the United States is the only country that has doctors, nurses and technicians out in these far-flung parts of the world.
A moment ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North suggested that we could set up a citizen to citizen organization in this country through which we might make our contributions individually. Such an organization is already in existence, with all due respect to his efforts. There is a national organization now with headquarters in Ottawa at 106 O'Connor Street and that is known as CARE. I received a copy of their 10th anniversary report in the mail. It shows that in this very field in which the Colombo plan is working, in the last 10 years they have distributed some $7 million. This has gone towards providing some equipment, aid to children and general rehabilitation in those countries that require aid similar to that for which the Colombo plan was designed. So, there is an organization and that is the address. Anyone who wants to make a contribution to any section of the world in which relief is needed will find that is an international organization set up for that purpose. The hon. member for Winnipeg North did not get the co-operation of the church organization, but the parishioners who were ready to gather $1,000 can send it in to CARE and parcels will be made up and shipped to any section of the world where assistance is needed. I am only trying to help the hon. member, I am not criticizing.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that is about all I wanted to say. I wanted to stress that we should take advantage of those agencies that have been set up around the United Nations. If we have anything to contribute to any section of the world there are these trained people heading up these different committees and commissions of the United Nations through which we should channel our contribution. Any section of the world that is getting relief should get it through the United Nations. As I have said many times, I do not think putting people on relief, nation by nation, is going to make any friends for us. It is like backing a note at the bank for one of your friends. He may be a good fellow, but he generally defaults on that note. He resents you forever after, so you have lost a friend and you have lost your money. I think that is equally true of Canada putting India or some other section of the world on 67509-437
Supply-External Affairs relief. If the relief is given through some United Nations agency, the money is channelled through it and you avoid duplication. Then, too, the proper organization gets the credit. We all contribute to the United Nations. I wish I had been in the house earlier for the minister's estimates because there are several things I would have liked to say. I will not say them now because they might open up a whole new series of speeches.

I will not add to the length of the debate or the erudition of the discussion with the few remarks I wish to make. I just want to say a very few words-if that phrase has any meaning now-to put something on the record which I think might be worth putting on the record. This refers to a petition I received from a United Church. When my petitioners receive this copy of Hansard, which I will send them, perhaps they will read the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North at the same time and perhaps his remarks will not fall on barren ground.
This is a petition from Washington United Church in Scarborough and reads as follows: Dear Mr. Enfield,
It has been brought to our attention that consideration is being given by the parliament of Canada to an increase of $9,000,000 in Canada's contribution to the Colombo plan. We, the undersigned members and adherents of Washington United Church, Scarborough, believing that moneys thus spent are well spent for peace, urge you to use your influence in support of this increase.
This petition is signed by over 51 members of the congregation and happily I was able to report to them that, although the increase was not $9 million it was $8 million and this is a very substantial increase indeed. I think this is the type of expression of opinion that is very important to us and very encouraging indeed. It comes to me unsolicited and as a complete surprise. It shows us all that the people of Canada

I think these people speak for the majority of the people in the country-are extremely interested in the type of help that we are giving under the Colombo plan, which is the finest type of help because it helps other people help themselves. I would encourage the government to carry on in their liberal attitude in this regard. I think we can spell "Liberal" with a large "L" and a small "1" in this context. The government should carry on its good work and gradually increase our contributions to the Colombo plan as long, of course, as they are consistent with common sense and good economy.

Just one question. I mentioned earlier that most of us were quite glad to see that the Colombo plan appropriation was increased by $1 million this year.

Supply-External Affairs As I recall what was said in the committee, actually this $8 million is not an increase for this year. As I understand it, most of this $8 million is to be expended on the atomic reactor to be built in Bombay, India. Actually, it will be spent in slightly more than two years. Therefore, there is not an $8-million appropriation for the coming year but rather it is to be spread over a period of time amounting to 28 months, I believe. Perhaps the minister might comment on that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I deal with that last point I would just like to say that I am in hearty agreement with all of the things that have been said in the house as to the value of the Colombo plan, both in terms of international friendship, political co-operation and economic aid, so that the underdeveloped countries may be able to help themselves.
I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South that it is undesirable to duplicate activities of this kind, and when otherwise practicable it is a good thing to do everything we can through the United Nations. But there is room, I think, for a commonwealth initiative such as the Colombo plan. It has, in certain respects, some advantages over the multilateral aid under the United Nations; although I certainly do not think there is any contradiction between the two because, under the Colombo plan, we can make arrangements directly with the country that we are assisting. We can share with the experts, the technicians and the workers of that particular country the construction of the project in question, and I think that has some obvious advantages. But we must not expect to get credit for these things. If we do these things merely in the hope that we are going to get a lot of credit, as my hon. friend said, we will be disappointed.
I think he suggested that the United States, in some of the pictures he had seen, was getting all the attention and therefore getting all the credit. I think there are a lot of Americans who would question how much credit they are getting in some of their activities in this field. That brings me to the point made by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris on the desirability of publicizing more what we are doing and, I am sure he meant by "we" not only Canada but other countries of the western world. He had a very important point there. I have had personal experience of the inadequacy of our own side in this regard. It is quite true that when you travel through Asia, if you happen to stop at a station in India, in Pakistan or in any Asian country, you will see a lot of literature, Marxist literature, or communist propaganda 

literature sometimes disguised, that sells commercially for a penny or two. It is very hard for some of the people in those countries to pay more than a penny or two, and it is very hard for them to find any literature expressing our way of life for a penny or two. There is obviously some subsidizing going on. I have more than once interested myself in this aspect of our general propaganda activities and I have often expressed the hope that we could form amongst ourselves, not as a government enterprise, but as a private enterprise, some kind of international book society which would devote itself to the distribution of that kind of good western literature well below cost with a subsidy which would be received from official sources.
I have now to go from the sublime almost to the ridiculous. We have increased our vote for books and subscriptions for presentation this year from, I think, $2,000 to $10,000. Therefore, we have $8,000 more with which to distribute literature on this subject.
Then, there is the last point raised by the hon. member for Oxford. The increase-and I share in the general satisfaction expressed about this increase-is $8 million this year. It could be more. There could always be more; but I am glad we have $8 million more, and it will enable us, I think, to increase our activities under the Colombo plan, with the qualification that has already been expressed that one of the difficulties is getting suitable experts, technical people, to carry out the projects which we already have under way. That $8 million is for the financial year. It is an additional appropriation for one year, but under our system, which has been approved by parliament, any unexpended funds during the year can be carried over and I think we have already about $3 million unexpended funds from a previous appropriation. It is expected that this $8 million will be spent during the next year.
Just one question: Is that $8 million entirely for the atomic reactor?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. It is
thought that this $8 million will take care of our expenditures for the atomic reactor, and probably more than take care of items in the coming year; but it is not earmarked specifically for that purpose. If we had not received this increase this year it might have been more difficult for us to undertake this additional commitment.
I am sorry to keep labouring this point. I realize the hour is getting on.
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, I want to go on but I shall wait until the noise stops. At

page 151 of the minutes of proceedings, No. 6, of the standing committee on external affairs, Mr. Cavell, in reply to a question of Mr. Michener, said:
No, it was last year. We had $25 million in the first two years and $26 million last year and that increase ol $1 million was provided tor technical assistance to countries to which we had not given technical assistance. The increase this year is from $26 million to $34 million and that takes care of the reactor to India which cost $7 million.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Chairman. If we had not obtained that increase we would not have been able to accept this extra commitment for the reactor without cutting down on some of our others. We expect to spend about $5 million this year on the reactor; but I do not think there is anything inconsistent between what I have said and what my hon. friend has read. We did not earmark the $34 million for any specific project in whole or in part, or any part of that money; but without that $8 million we might have found difficulty in carrying out the existing projects in which we are engaged and adding to them.

Mr. Chairman, I think there is general agreement in the house that the provision for aid under the Colombo plan is a good one. There are some of us who would like to see such provisions made through the United Nations. Whenever, for some reason or another, it does not appear feasible, we certainly support a commonwealth program like the Colombo plan.
I do not think that in the general field of economic assistance Canada is measuring up. I believe that in relation to the needs of the world, in relation to the needs of democracy, in relation to Canada's ability to provide assistance, we are doing a dismally poor job. Even with the increase in the Colombo plan provision our contribution is just over $2 per capita for the year under review. It is something less than one-seventh of one per cent of our gross national product.
I was amazed at the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William when he said that as far as he himself was concerned until the government did something to improve the lot of a certain group of Canadians he was opposed to any further increase in provisions under the Colombo plan.
I do not think any modern nation would be making progress in the world today if its governing representatives took the attitude that until a given situation were improved they would not do anything to help anybody. I think the hon. member's view is one that is not shared by a majority of Canadians.
I have taken some interest in the Colombo plan for some time. I do not know all the
67509-437J
Supply-External Affairs details concerning how it operates but I am aware that certain allocations have been made to counterpart funds, as they are called, in the past. According to the minutes of the external affairs committee for June 7, 1955, steam locomotives valued at $23; million were sent to India and the account had been set up as a counterpart fund. The same is true of trucks, buses and workshop machinery valued at $4 million, copper and aluminum valued at $5 million, and so on. Under the Colombo plan in the past certain provisions of grain have been made to India totalling $15 million, to Pakistan totalling $5 million and flour valued at $1,300,000 was sent to Ceylon.
I would like to learn from the minister what has been done recently under the Colombo plan to explore with India, Pakistan, Ceylon aid other nations that participate in the plan the possibility and practicability of making additional funds available for the purchase of food from Canada and the provision of that food along the same lines followed in the past.
There can be no argument to the effect that Canada does not have the food. The crop year is just ending and while these are tentative estimates it has been estimated that even with the increased sales in the crop year just ended the carryover of Canadian wheat will be up some 23 million bushels. Although the prospects for a large Canadian crop of wheat were rather doubtful six weeks ago it now appears that if good weather conditions prevail over the next four weeks the chances are this year Canada will produce only slightly less wheat than was produced last year. There is no question about our not having an abundance of wheat. The question is, can India use additional quantities of wheat?
India is not receiving any wheat from Canada now. In the crop year just ended India did not purchase a single bushel of wheat from Canada for the first time in many years. In 1951 India obtained 18 million bushels of wheat from Canada, 14 mih lion in 1952, 4 million in 1953 and in the period 1954-55 the purchase dropped to 2.3 million bushels.
From information I have been able to obtain I believe India wants more wheat and needs more food. As a matter of fact, an associated press report which appeared in Canadian newspapers on June 28 last indicated:
India today announced its decision to open negotiations with the United States for the purchase of 3 million tons of wheat worth more than $200 million.

Supply-External Affairs
That would amount to negotiations tor "the purchase of a quantity in excess of 100 million bushels of wheat. The report went [DOT]on to say:
Informed sources said India hopes to obtain as .much wheat as possible under the U.S. surplus program which would enable India to pay rupees and then borrow the money back for economic development projects.
It would appear from this report that India is entering into negotiations with the United States to obtain a large quantity of United States wheat under precisely the same type of arrangement by which India purchased substantial quantities of wheat from Canada a few years ago.
I am asking the minister if the Colombo plan officials have discussed with India and other nations involved in the plan whether they need additional food and whether the Canadian government would be prepared to provide additional funds in order that such food may be made available?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have discussed with the Indian, Pakistani and Ceylon governments on accasion the provision of food under the Colombo plan and it has been agreed that the Colombo plan should not be used for that purpose except in a case of emergency and that it should be restricted to its original aim which was the provision of capital and technical assistance.
It is quite true that we have provided Pakistan and India with wheat-I think in 1952 and 1953-for which counterpart funds were set up, but those were during emergency food conditions. I think there was a famine condition in India at that time and we were requested by India as an exception to the agreed principle to provide food under the Colombo plan. They have made it quite clear to us that normally they would prefer to receive our help under the plan in the form of capital and technical assistance.
One form that assistance takes is in irrigation and power projects. We have participated in such projects. The irrigation part of these projects makes possible the growth of food in the country concerned. We have made it possible notably in the Mayurakshi project, for hundreds of thousands of agricultural acres to be brought under cultivation. In the long run that is of much more help to India than sending food directly from Canada.
It is also my information that India had a good crop this year and does not require wheat to meet the needs of her own people. She may have made a special arrangement under advantageous financial circumstances with the United States; however, I am not aware of it. The Colombo plan was not
fMr. Argue.]
designed for this purpose and we have been told by the three governments in question that they would much prefer our contribution to take the form of capital and technical assistance under the Colombo plan.

I do not know whether or not the minister understood my question. I was not asking him whether the money now appropriated under the Colombo plan or any part of it could be used for the purchases I referred to. I can well understand the position of India that they would be prepared to tighten their belts today in order to go forward with irrigation and other development projects in order that they might have an abundance of food in the future.
My question was this. Has any consideration been given in discussions with India as to whether she would purchase substantial quantities of grain from this country if our government were prepared to allocate funds in addition to the funds that are now being discussed?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I am sorry if I misunderstood my hon. friend. To my knowledge we have not discussed additional funds to be provided under the Colombo plan for this particular purpose with any Colombo plan government.

Did I understand the minister to say when he was speaking formerly that India has no need for wheat in the immediate future? If that is the case, is the minister saying that India is not now undertaking negotiations with the United States for the purchase of an extremely large quantity of wheat, namely over 100 million bushels?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I did not say that, Mr. Chairman. I am not acquainted with that particular negotiation. When the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce are under discussion they will deal with exports of wheat specifically and my hon. friend can no doubt obtain some information concerning that aspect of the question.
All I have said is that while we are anxious to sell wheat wherever we can, and India is included in the countries with which we would like to do business, I have been informed that India had a good crop year and this makes it unlikely that she would want to obtain much wheat from Canada.
I went on to say that we had not discussed with India or any other country an increase of this kind to our appropriations under the Colombo plan because the Colombo plan was not designed for that purpose. The Colombo plan was designed for the provision of technical and capital assistance.

Supply-External Affairs

Someone in the government is falling down very badly. I am surprised that, with the plans under the Colombo plan, such a discussion, at any rate an exploratory discussion, has not taken place. The minister said that India does not require wheat, but in the crop year just ended a few days ago, according to the very latest report, whilst India did not purchase a single bushel of Canadian wheat in that crop year, it purchased from the United States 10,170,000 bushels and from Australia 6,170,000 bushels. So India is buying wheat. India is buying wheat from countries other than Canada, and India is now, according to this report, having discussions with the United States to get a very large quantity of wheat and on precisely the same kind of terms as Canada dealt with India a few years ago.

I am interested in this discussion between the minister and the hon. member for Assiniboia. I have been interested in the Colombo plan for years. I am very glad to see the increase in the appropriation. I believe that it will be all to the good to make available larger funds for the work which, the minister said, is so well in hand. I am also inclined to believe that the Colombo plan was never designed for the purpose of distributing relief foods for other products. I can understand the anxiety of the hon. member for Assiniboia in the light of the fact that we have a very large surplus of wheat in our country.
And these negotiations with the United States.

And the negotiations that have gone on with the United States, but I am also of the opinion that the distribution of surplus products and commodities ought to take place through such an organization as was envisaged by the Food and Agriculture Organization a few years ago: an international commodity clearing house. Until we get such an organization set up and working effectively, I am afraid that we shall go on as we are at the present time, with countries needing and going without while other countries have their large surpluses, and perhaps surpluses that may eventually be destroyed or deteriorate. If we press more strongly for the international commodity clearing house, which was turned down some years ago-
And by this government.
Unfortunately, it was not pressed too strongly by the government.
The government opposed it.

But I can quite understand the position of the minister in connection with the Colombo plan. These funds are made
available more for capital assistance, the purpose being to make it possible for the people who are the beneficiaries of the plan to help themselves; not so much to bring relief at the moment. I think that is what they want: capital assistance, the building of works, increasing their capability of production. I think that is right. I can understand why the minister would hesitate to offer much encouragement that we could distribute our surplus wheat under the Colombo plan, but I think the hon. member for Assiniboia is quite right in pressing for the recognition of a need there. That need is growing, and it seems to be daily more impressive.
In the meantime they should! have all the bread they need.

I think that is correct. As long as there is surplus food in the world, certainly it should be made available through some means to the needy people. There is great virtue in some of the things said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North earlier this afternoon. He thought that gifts of produce, foods and other things, from people to people would be the ideal arrangement. I think it would be, too, if you could get the people to do it.
We have got into the habit of looking to the government for almost everything. If anything goes wrong, we say that the government is to blame. However, frankly I believe that such a thing as providing relief to other nations could very well be undertaken by private agencies and the citizens of a country where the surpluses exist. I can see the possibility of forming an organization of the people themselves. That has been done; I have seen it done. Our people for many years -and when I say "our people" I mean my own church group in particular-have formed what we call a church welfare program. Under that program we co-operate in building up a stockpile of all kinds of produce. That is not the general stockpile of the nation; that is supplementary to the stockpiles of the nation, one we build up as a consequence of a co-operative effort amongst ourselves and in our spare time. That is set aside, put into warehouses and prepared thoroughly; what has to be preserved is preserved, and so on. We had done this for years and, when world war II was over, within hours we had trainloads of those goods on their way to the seaboard where they were trans-shipped and sent to Europe and distributed as from our people to the people there who needed them. There was no thought of getting credit for it. We thought only of making available to those people, out of the surplus of goods we had, enough to keep them from starving.

Supply-External Affairs
That principle is good. It is a sound principle, and particularly what it would do for the people who produce and made available the commodities is something we cannot possibly estimate. It would be far more effective than if we looked to the government to do it all. Just the same, in relation to this business of distributing surpluses of produce, particularly foods, throughout the world, we need the international commodity clearing house set up. The sooner we can get it, the better it will be. I commend the minister and his department on what they have been doing with regard to the Colombo plan. It has been something you could not have done through the United Nations, with all the intransigence of some of the members of the United Nations. It is filling a tremendous need, and the people who are the beneficiaries of it are remembering that Canada is putting up a sizeable sum of money each year, which can be increased, I am sure, as technical assistance and technical direction are made available so that the money is properly spent. I agree with that principle.

I had not intended to
say anything on this matter until my hon. friend from Assiniboia raised this rather interesting suggestion. However, since he has done so, I should possibly say, to begin with, that over the years I have been a most strong supporter on behalf of an increase in the amounts being expended under the Colombo plan.
I have a strong recollection of an occasion in 1951 when, having been in Australia and New Zealand and having met there with representatives of India, Ceylon and countries in the other commonwealth areas in Asia, I returned to Canada and asked that the amount then being expended on behalf of the Colombo plan, which was $25 million, should be doubled if Canada was to take its place among the nations of the commonwealth in preserving and maintaining our defences against the on-rush of communism. Over and over again at the parliamentary conference in Australia and New Zealand the representatives of those countries warned us that, unless material assistance of this type was forthcoming, in a few years communism, by its propaganda and by its promises of improving the economic lot of the peoples of those countries, would make invasions into the hearts and souls of the peoples of those countries to a degree that might never be retrieved by the free world.
Having said that, I come to the suggestion of my hon. friend with regard to wheat marketing. I am at one with him that we should do anything that is necessary in order to secure markets for our surplus products,

and in particular for our wheat. However, from that point on I do not follow the same path as he has followed. He suggests that we should get into line with what the United States is doing. To me that is a dangerous course to follow.
What the United States is doing is simply this. With its vast surpluses of wheat, cotton and the like it is going to underprivileged areas in various parts of the world, making available amounts of these surpluses and receiving a credit in the form of local guarantees and then using these local guarantees for economic assistance in those countries. What the United States is doing in fact by that policy is breaking up the markets for farm commodities all over the world. It is part and parcel of its giveaway, fire sale assistance agricultural policy.
That is where an orderly system of international distribution would be helpful.

Some aspects of the
Uniied States disposal plan mean disorderly distribution. The plan is having its effect and to some degree has disturbed Canada's markets for agricultural products in various parts of the world. I believe that the only way in which we can hope to compete against that policy so dangerous to Canadian agriculture would be through the medium of advances to these NATO countries with which advances purchases of our wheat and other products can be made.
What we have been condemning has been the United States attitude of going throughout the world without regard to its responsibilities under GATT and NATO and under the guise of this plan undermining our markets for agricultural products. I think it would be a dangerous course to follow to endeavour to emulate the United States in this regard. What I believe should be done is to protest to the United States government, as members on this side of the house have asked over and over again, against a policy so dangerous to the maintenance of a free economy among the free nations and so detrimental to those countries that are joined together in freedom in the marketing of their agricultural products.
In saying that I am all for the objective that the hon. gentleman has in mind, but I must say that I believe that for us to imitate the United States in this regard would be detrimental and dangerous to future farm markets, in particular markets for Canada's wheat, and would be using the Colombo plan in a manner that was never contemplated.
One of the aspects of the Colombo plan to which our attention was directed by representatives from India and Pakistan was

that the cost of transportation of wheat and wheat products was so high as to render practically useless the importation of these commodities except in emergency cases. What they wanted was some form of material assistance that would enable them in their own countries to transform areas at present unproductive into productive areas, thereby enabling them to meet their own needs.
While I am altogether in favour of the objective of the hon. gentleman, I am afraid that in adopting the course he has suggested we would be in fact following a course which we have been condemning on the part of the United States and with respect to which I for one have suggested over and over again to the government that the strongest note should be sent to the United States government indicating that by that course they are undermining the free economy of the world and denying Canada and other nations joined with them in freedom the opportunity to maintain the strongest and most effective agricultural organizations.

I believe that the hon. member for Assiniboia perhaps did not understand what I said. Probably an Irishman needs a second chance to make himself clear. I congratulated the minister on the increase of $8 million. I support the United Nations completely, just as strongly as anybody in the house, but I think that next year we should give the first consideration to retired civil servants who have not got enough to live on. I support that before I will support any further increase in our contribution to the Colombo plan over and above the $8 million. I think that is quite clear.

I think the member for Prince Albert has completely misunderstood and misinterpreted what I have said. He said, as I understood him, that I was advocating the same kind of policy as the United States, and I said nothing of the sort.
I thought you did.

I said nothing of the sort because, as I believe the hon. member for Prince Albert well knows, the Americans do not have just the one so-called give-away policy but have policies under three different acts of congress.
That is one of the means.

This is not a give-away program at all. According to the report I read to the house, the Americans are not giving anything away. It is not a give-away. All the indignation that the member for Prince Albert was able to generate was completely misdirected because I did not say anything like what he said I did. However, if you
Supply-External Affairs are going to say that the whole United States policy is wrong and that Canada should not do any of the things the United States is doing-I emphasize "any"-then it means that we say to the nations of the world that unless they have hard currency, unless they have dollars, they can starve to death because we are going to keep our wheat until they find the dollars.
I do not agree with that kind of policy. We have lost the Indian market for Canadian wheat. In the last crop year just ended a couple of days ago we did not sell or send a single bushel of Canadian wheat to India, and that is what I think is wrong. I think we should adopt policies that will not only enable us to dispose of Canadian grain but will also enable us to do our part to see that the people of India, who are hungry and need grain, have a chance to obtain grain.
I want to say that the farm organizations support this point of view. The Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Alberta wheat pool, the Manitoba wheat pool and the Interprovincial Farm Union Council support this point of view. They say that wherever a nation is in need of wheat and has not the currency- the dollars-with which to purchase the wheat, Canada should negotiate with such country to the end that we may be able to accept their currency and to provide them with a reasonable quantity of Canadian wheat over a period of time. That is precisely, as I understand it, what India is endeavouring to do with the United States. It is the same thing precisely as we did under the Colombo plan a few years ago, namely provide wheat, set up counterpart funds and pay the Canadian producer for the wheat and by that means assist in economic aid and economic development.
I want to assure the hon. member for Prince Albert that I had no intention of saying that we should adopt the United States wheat policy, and I do not believe the record will show that I said that.

Mr. Chairman, may I say just one word. I am surprised at the use of the expression "indignation". There was no indignation. It was simply argument. When my hon. friend says that this is the plan of the farmers union and these other organizations, may I say that I do not believe that it is. What these organizations said is this. They said that we should take foreign currencies-that is soft currencies-for our wheat and sell for those currencies. But what the United States is doing is accepting the currency of India-and then using that currency in India for the amelioration of conditions in India. That is quite a different

Supply-External Affairs proposition from the one that has been advanced on the part of the organizations to which my hon. friend has made reference. What this plan on the part of the United States simply amounts to is this: The United States has available many millions of dollars for economic assistance abroad. It says to the countries In question, in effect:	We are
going to give you this assistance. You accept our wheat or other surplus agricultural products. We will take your money. Then we will use that money within your territory, within the limitations imposed by the agricultural laws of the United States, in order to raise conditions and to improve the economic lot of your country. What it amounts to, in fact, is that the United States is granting direct assistance to those countries in the billions of dollars. It uses this means as one of three methods to assist needy nations and at the same time dispose of its surpluses.
