114. Contribution to the United Nations relief and works agency for Palestine refugees in the Near East, $500,000.

This is a contribution for a grant to the United Nations relief and works agency for Palestine refugees in the Near East. In this regard I should like to ask the minister what if any advance has been made during the last year to meet the extremely serious problem created by these refugee camps in Arab countries. As one visits these camps one cannot but be impressed by the need for their existence while at the same time realizing that they constitute festering sores among the individuals occupying them. Has any advance been made in the last year towards the demobilization of these refugee people? How many were in these camps a year ago? To what degree has there been any decrease during the last year? Has the minister any message of hope that this, one of the darkest blots on the probability of maintaining peace in the middle east, may be obliterated and removed?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am more anxious than confident about the nature of this problem and a solution if it. As my hon. friend has said, it is a desperate problem. It is a desperate problem economically for those concerned and it is a dangerous problem politically. In those refugee camps in Palestine I think there are about 905,000 refugees. I think that number is greater than it was when this problem first faced us. The contributions that are being made to this fund are for the purpose of relief, in order to keep these refugees alive, and also for the more constructive purpose of rehabilitation and resettlement. Not so much has been done

in the latter category because the activities that have been under way for purposes of rehabilitation and resettlement have been bedevilled by the political difficulties which it seems will have to be solved before rehabilitation can take place. Some progress has been made by the agency in developing a works program-the Sinai Works Program- and some refugees have been settled in works projects of one kind and another. But there has been a very inadequate response to the challenge of this problem. The larger project of the Jordan dam which would take care of a good many of these refugees and give them employment is not likely to be implemented as long as political conditions remain as unhappy as they are. With great reluctance I say that we feel that in making a contribution to this problem now we are not making a very constructive one because about all we are doing is keeping these people alive. However, someone must do that. We must hope that future developments will make possible both rehabilitation and resettlement. So far as resettlement is concerned, that aspect of the problem is complicated by the fact that the refugees themselves want to go back to Israel. There is not room there for all of them, in and around Israel, and I doubt whether it is possible to find a solution by wholesale repatriation there, although the state of Israel has agreed to receive some. The other way to solve this problem of resettlement is to find other parts of the world-that is of the Arab world and other places-where they might be resettled. The refugees themselves are showing great reluctance to leave the camps for that purpose and are not being encouraged to do so by the Arab governments. That is all I can say, Mr. Chairman. I am afraid it is not a very encouraging report.

I should like to ask the minister this question. Is there any possibility of increasing the amount so that these people can get a more adequate allowance than they are getting at the present time? According to reports that we receive-and there has been very excellent commentation here through the C.B.C. recently-it is not adequate. Is there any possibility of United Nations increasing this amount so that these people will not be left so much on the verge of starvation? Apparently the amount that is given is, according to our standards, terrifically low.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is true, Mr. Chairman; but my information is that the condition of the refugees in the camps-though rather deplorable, no doubt, when comparison is made with our own standards-is as good as if not better than that of those Arabs in the

same position outside the camps. I do not think there is any foundation for the stories that go around to the effect that the refugees in these camps are on starvation diets, and that sort of thing. That is not the case. They are not badly looked after.

Mr. Chairman, I can vouch for the truth of what the minister has just said. All one has to do is to visit some of the Arab settlements that are outside the camps. He will see that those who are inside the camps or the compounds are not being too badly treated by comparison. Indeed, the horrible thing about the camps is that these people are deteriorating year by year. They have been in there now since 1948 and they have become completely dependent. As the minister said, it grows worse daily. It looks to me as though the United Nations organization will have to be prepared to spend a considerable sum of money in developing some settlement schemes in Syria, Jordan and the other Arab states.
One of the things it seems to me they could be doing is to develop the potential irrigation projects out of the waters that come down from northern Syria. There is a lot of land that could be irrigated and made habitable for these people. If they are given a chance to settle on a piece of land where there is some water, I feel quite sure that in a few years at least they will put themselves on an equal basis with the Arab peoples elsewhere. I am quite sure that Israel is not prepared to take them back, not only because there is no room but because a good many of these people took up arms against the government of Israel in the war of liberation in 1948 and therefore are guilty of treason in the true sense of the word, so they could hardly take them back. This does not for one moment, or should not at any rate, militate against every effort being made to see that they are being rehabilitated in a proper manner.
I can understand what a difficult problem it is when you can get the full co-operation of the governments of the Arab states, but you have not got it. How you are to get it is a problem. May I right here issue a word of warning? We in the western world have done so much now to lose the friendship of the Arab states generally that I think we had better be careful of the sort of sanctions we attempt to impose for the purpose of getting this rehabilitation complete. Just the same, it is a great humanitarian problem that has to be solved somehow.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We had hoped that we would have discharged our responsibilities in IndoChina by now as a member of the international commission, but that has not been possible. As my hon. friend knows, there are three commissions. The one in Cambodia has had its activities reduced greatly. Military teams have been disbanded and we have merely a skeleton military and external affairs staff in the capital. We would, I think, have been able to withdraw completely from Cambodia by now but for the fact there is a connection in the Geneva agreement between the three commissions.
The commission in Laos has not been able to complete its work because of the difficulty of absorbing the two northern provinces now under Pathet Lao communist control into the state of Laos. The commission is doing its best to bring that about because if these provinces remain under communist control and the communists become established there, it would be an unhappy development.
So far as the Viet Nam commission is concerned, under the Geneva arrangement elections were to have been held by July 20 of this year, this has not been possible because the government of South Viet Nam, the Diem government, has not been willing to accept the legal responsibilities that were accepted by the French under the Geneva agreement. French troops and French authorities have now withdrawn from South Viet Nam. Negotiations are going on now by which we hope the Diem government will accept in practice, if not in theory, certain responsibilities under the Geneva agreement which will enable the commission to carry on. The other difficulty is the understandable reluctance on the part of the Diem government to take part

616. Departmental administration-further amount required, $121,199.

That is what I thought. My hon. friend the hon. member for Broadview brought up a question some hours ago with regard to the treatment accorded to Mr. Milan Babic, who was travelling on a Canadian passport and who, according to the telegram my hon. friend read to the committee this afternoon, was forced to submit to two hours of interrogation. In addition to that, he had to wait overnight until word was received from Washington to permit of his clearance being granted. I should like to know from the minister what justification there is for more than a mere cursory examination being made of a person travelling under a Canadian passport, having arrived in the United States and having no intention to do more than pass through the United States to his Canadian destination. Is such a person not entitled to receive more courteous and considerate treatment than was accorded to this man? According to the Associated Press dispatch from New York on July 31, this man's name was on a list which called for close check by the service. A spokesman said a name may be placed on the list for 101 reasons. Sir, most of us would be satisfied with one of those reasons being explained.
Why was this man treated in this way? Does a Canadian passport not convey to the holder certain rights which were apparently violated in this case? Was this an examination that applied to a Canadian any of the principles of McCarthyism? Why should a Canadian, once the Canadian government has seen fit, through its Secretary of State for External Affairs, to grant him a passport, be required to be examined as to whether or not he is a fit and proper person, since he has been so designated and considered by the
[Mr. Pearson.l

Canadian government, before a passport is issued? I would appreciate it if the minister would advise the committee of the latest information on this question, because it is one that has aroused a considerable amount of feeling in our country. I am sure that such feelings should be appeased at the earliest possible date.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I advised the house, I have already sent a telegram to this naturalized Canadian in order to get his version of the facts as they have been related in the press. So far as I know a reply to that telegram has not yet been received, although I have had a chance to see the telegram that he sent to my hon. friend opposite who brought this matter up earlier. I would say that on the basis of the information that I have already received there appears to be no justification whatever for the treatment that was given this shipwrecked Canadian when he reached New York.
Of course, the possession of a Canadian passport does not give anyone immunity from the investigations and the attentions of the representative and the officials of a foreign government once the holder of that Canadian passport reaches the land of that foreign government. As I said yesterday, the United States has the legal right to question and to detain anybody on its soil. A legal right is one thing, propriety and justice are something else. I do not feel that the United States authorities should have taken the action they did take in these circumstances. We have been informed by those authorities that he was treated and questioned with courtesy. In that respect the information which appeared in the press does not coincide with that which we have been given by the officials of the United States government.
We were also informed, Mr. Chairman, that this particular man, for some reason or other and I do not know why-was on some security list of the United States and that was why he was singled out for this special attention. After the case was cleared up, I believe through intervention from Washington, he was allowed to proceed.
I am not going to challenge the right of any government to detain any foreigner on its soil if it has a legitimate reason for detaining him on security grounds. But we have no reason to believe that this particular Canadian was a security risk in any country. He is certainly not on any security list of ours, and therefore I regret very much that he should have been subjected to this kind of treatment. After we hear from Mr. Babic himself, if the facts of his own message indicate that it should be done, we shall

follow this matter up by protesting to the United States authorities in Washington.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to go into this matter at this particular moment in very great detail and I wonder whether my hon. friend, who is always so considerate in these matters, would agree if I sent him a pretty full and complete written report on this whole question of the package deal? I will, however, say to him now in answer to his particular questions, that the policy of the government in this matter was stated long before the United Nations assembly met in New York and therefore we were not, as he rather suggested this morning, doing something behind the backs of the people of this country, who had no reason to believe that we were taking this stand.
I said previous to the assembly of last year that we supported the principle of universality of membership. So we did support at the United Nations assembly all outstanding applications for membership in the United Nations except those on behalf of states which were divided. Those applications included some strongly anti-communist states like Japan, Italy,. Spain, Austria and Ireland. It included some states that we call now uncommitted, and it included some communist states. In order to get our friends into the United Nations-and we thought they certainly should be there-Japan was one of them-we had to accept the whole list that I have mentioned, and an arrangement was made that all of those countries should be brought into the United Nations at this time. That arrangement was not carried out because the government of nationalist China, at the security council, vetoed Outer Mongolia, and because of that fact the Soviet union vetoed Japan. But the rest of them were admitted, and I think, with respect to my hon. friend, there is a good deal to be said-notwithstanding the views we may have about the governments of some of those countries-for having them as sovereign states in the United Nations. At least that is the view that we took at that time.
Supply-External Affairs

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to be difficult about this matter. I shall welcome the full statement that the minister will send me but I do believe the people of Canada are entitled to be able to read some details in Hansard about this whole experience we went through, especially as we find such statements as the one I propose to quote from the Daily Mirror of New York of December 15, 1955, which in an editorial referring to this matter of the package deal said:
It was an obvious, childish trick to get Red China into the United Nations by subterfuge.
This paper is not a minor paper in the United States; I think it has over 2 million circulation and is rather reputable. The editor and the staff were right there where they were able to follow the whole situation right through. This particular editorial, which is entitled, "The United Nations Veto", closes with these words:
Canada is also at fault for serving Russia's purposes, even if unwittingly.
This is a pretty strong indication, I would say, that it is important to have some explanation. Here is another editorial entitled, "Suggestion for Dulles". I do not know whether this is the same paper-no, it is another paper. It is one called The News. In its editorial are these words, reporting Nationalist China's delegate T. F. Tsiang:
As U.N. Nationalist China delegate T. F. Tsiang says, four of these are nothing but captive nations of the red slave empire:	Albania, Bulgaria,
Hungary and Romania.
By letting them in, Dr. Tsiang adds, the U.N. in effect recognized their present robber governments and promised never to lift a finger to help free these enslaved peoples. For that, Tsiang doubts the slaves "will ever forgive us".
As I said before the committee recessed for lunch, it looks to me as though in recognizing Mongolia we recognized first of all that red Russia has a claim to Mongolia which I do not see how she can possibly establish, and second that she has a right to take any province of Russia and erect it into an independent nation and have it admitted to the United Nations.
Under such a rule it ought to be possible for the United States to gain admission to the United Nations for everyone of the 48 states and Alaska as independent nations. It also ought to be possible for Canada to gain admission for every one of the ten provinces in this country; but I will wager that if we made a request or even hinted that Ontario, for example, should be admitted into the United Nations there would be plenty of protest forthcoming from Russia and many other nations.

Supply-External Affairs
That is a serious principle, too. In addition to that, the admission of outer Mongolia into the United Nations is tantamount to saying that this section of territory no longer belongs to nationalist China and she has no claim to it whatever.
Every one of the assumptions I have mentioned is an unsound assumption. No matter how we may look at it, there is still in effect a state of war between nationalist China and red China because they have never come to terms nor agreed to a treaty. That is a serious matter. If we are going to go forward in the world with any principles of international fair dealing we will have to give consideration to matters of this kind.
There has been a great deal of suggestion on the part of Canadian authorities-more or less veiled, ambiguous and in a form that could be denied-and a great deal of pressure for the recognition of red China. It is pointed out that Great Britain has recognized red China and consequently we should do the same. I feel that in the interests of international fair dealing and the stability of moral principles we should draw up a standard and a set of principles which would have to be met by a nation in order to have it be worthy of recognition and admission to the United Nations.
I do not believe communist China could qualify under any combination of valid principles as being worthy of entering the United Nations. I have no desire to labour this point but those people who are interested in pursuing this matter in a scientific way might with some profit read my House of Commons speech of April 21, 1955 and my House of Commons speech of May 5, 1955. They will find plenty of evidence and authorities to back up my statements. I will challenge any man on earth to question the conclusions which are drawn in those two speeches or the authorities which are used.
They show beyond a question of doubt that China was simply stolen from Chiang Kai-shek. Communists and members of the United States communist organization, working through the United States state department, are guilty of robbing Chiang Kai-shek of China. There is evidence beyond any possibility of question that such was the case. In the light of those considerations I say that while the minister has given a reply it is far from being an adequate answer. I think it leaves the whole international situation absolutely awash. No community of people knows where it stands.
Personally I object to Canada being a party to the recognition of principles which in the history of this world up to the present time have never been deemed valid by any

reputable nation. People may say, "Well, the reds are in charge of China; they are the government de facto. What are you going to do about it?" This amounts to saying that if a gang of robbers carries off 1,000 steers into the mountains and holds them there for a year the gang of robbers owns the steers. I do not think anyone will recognize any validity in that assumption.
Now, may I say a word or two concerning what did occur in connection with China? I do not wish to go into too much detail concerning what did occur in connection with China but one or two of these considerations must be taken into account, it seems to me. Franklin D. Roosevelt at the Yalta conference in February 1945 granted Stalin rights to Manchuria which gave Stalin a chance to overrun all of China unless China was ably assisted by those countries she had already befriended, such as the United States.
What conceivable right had Roosevelt, who was visiting from the United States, to make any commitments whatsoever in respect of land which he had no right to by any conceivable stretch of the imagination? Fundamentally, however, it was that commitment upon which Russia acted and this put Chiang Kai-shek in a set of circumstances from which it would have been difficult to extricate himself.
Harry S. Truman followed up that course of action at the Potsdam conference and confirmed that commitment. Again, what right had Truman doing that? From that point on some of the most treacherous manipulations, scheming and downright interference from the United States took place, as in the case of General Marshall, who was sent over to China in 1946 by the United States administration with the express mission of stopping Chiang Kai-shek from driving the red communists back into Russia.
By the most disreputable and disgraceful set of actions, the United States, under the guidance of Dean Acheson, succeeded in putting Chiang Kai-shek into a position in which he had to withdraw to Formosa. Then apparently the Korean war was brought on by the administration of the U.S.A. with the calculated purpose of giving the United States an excuse for putting the U.S. seventh fleet in the strait so that Chiang Kai-shek could not possibly go back to the Chinese mainland and recover it, notwithstanding the fact that, when Chiang Kai-shek withdrew, he left 1,250,000 loyal, fully-trained soldiers in China, facing the communists there, he left 150 million loyal Chinese on the west and southern borders of China, and with his navy he was able to blockade and prevent ships from going up and supplying the north red

China people with munitions, and with his air force of 250 aircraft he was able to deliver goods to support his 1,250,000 soldiers on the Chinese mainland.
There are people who revolt at the idea of saying that the south Korean war was engineered. The evidence to support that presumption is so strong that I believe that any judge of any reputation whatsoever would rule that, on the basis of circumstantial evidence, the south Korean war was engineered, by the United States administration and for no purpose whatsoever other than to prevent Chiang Kai-shek from getting back on the Chinese mainland and reconquering China, and at the same time also to let Russia get control of south Korea.
I do not wish to labour this any further but I certainly think that we should have no more tormenting and tantalizing of any Canadian government official, from the Prime Minister right down, urging that red China be recognized. The Chinese are just a group of red robbers. They do not undertake to keep any treaty. What they are doing now in Burma, according to the reports, if we can rely on them, indicates that what I have said is true, that they are just a lot of robbers. I think I have said enough to show that I have good reason for bringing this matter up. I shall take up the minister's promise and accept the material he sends me and read it through with great care, and probably next year I shall talk to him again about this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On July 12, when we were able to devote about ten minutes to the study of these estimates, I had time to make a general statement, and then I said I wished to place before the house a statement of our fundamental concepts and policy in administering the national parks of Canada.
I believe that the first question that we should ask ourselves is: what are, in fact, the national parks of Canada? I believe we have across our country a system of national parks that are second to none. There are 17 of these parks from British Columbia to Nova Scotia, and it is likely that one other will be added in the near future in the province of Newfoundland. They have a total area of more than 29,000 square miles. They contain examples of the finest scenic beauties in mountain, forest and water that can be found anywhere. They provide refuge for wildlife where it can be seen and enjoyed under natural conditions. Some of the older parks such as Banff and Jasper have become famous throughout the world. Above all, the parks provide Canadians in all walks of life with beautiful areas preserved for all time for their benefit and enjoyment.
The next question, and it is very important that we ask these questions of ourselves from time to time because of the requests we have to build and make various installations in the parks, is: why do we have the parks? Year after year, the members of this house have shown strong interest in the further development of the national parks, in having them made more available and enjoyable for the Canadian people. Today there are few who do not recognize and appreciate the value of the parks, but this was not always the case. Years ago, both in Canada and the United States, many persons interested in the exploitation of natural resources looked on the establishment of parks for the use of the people as a foolish dream and a waste of potential profit for themselves. It is to the credit of our legislators in the past that they had the foresight to see the needs of the future and to ensure for us the preservation of that great heritage which is ours in the national parks of Canada today.

Supply-Northern Affairs
We hear so much now about the parks in the travel advertising; we hear so much about their value to the tourist industry, the stimulus they provide to draw tourists from outside Canada, the contribution the parks make through the tourist and other industries to the general economy of Canada, that it would almost seem that the parks were created for the economic benefits they bestow. How far people can depart, even in this day and age, from the ideal that inspired our fathers and forefathers and that, I am convinced, rests firmly in the hearts of the great majority of Canadians who know and love the parks and who know why they have been established.
The parks are dedicated under the National Parks Act to the benefit, education and enjoyment of the Canadian people, and the act requires that they be used and maintained in such a way that they will be left unimpaired for the benefit of future generations.
The parks were not established for the tourist industry; they were not established for commercial pursuits, or for their direct and indirect economic benefits. They were established, I repeat, for the benefit, education and enjoyment of the Canadian people. They were established so that Canadians would have for all time great areas where they could relax and renew their strength in settings of unrivalled beauty.
To be sure, there is value to Canada in the industries that derive benefits from the parks, but infinitely greater is the value our people derive, in their hundreds of thousands, in happier minds and healthier bodies gained through rest and recreation in our great park areas. The important reasons, therefore, that we have the national parks are: first, to provide unspoiled areas, and I draw this to the attention of a number of members who sometimes make suggestions for installations in parks which will spoil the parks. Our aim is to provide unspoiled areas where people can enjoy rest and recreation in surroundings that are a complete change from what they meet in their normal lives; to provide unspoiled areas where people can enjoy and appreciate the God-given beauties and wonders that we in Canada are fortunate to possess as part of our national heritage; to provide unspoiled areas wherein people can learn about the world of nature, and become better people through the knowledge that there are other things in life of importance apart from man's creations. It is obvious that the value of the parks to the Canadian people rests more in the realm of the spirit than in the realm of commerce, and that this value of the parks can be lost forever unless they are preserved unspoiled and unimpaired to the greatest possible extent.
[Mr. Lesage.l

How then, Mr. Chairman, should we approach the administration of these parks? In the United States, where the pressure of population on land use and a growing appreciation of conservation principles led to the establishment of a great parks system even earlier than in Canada, the fundamental value of the parks was fully realized by many public spirited citizens, even when commercial interests were fighting the creation of the parks with every instrument at their disposal. In 1918 the then secretary of the interior, Franklin K. Lane, set out the basic principles behind the parks in these words:
First, the national parks must be maintained in absolutely unimpaired form for the use of future generations as well as those of our time.
Second, they are set apart for the use, observation, health and pleasure of the people.
Third, the national interest must dictate all decisions affecting public or private enterprise in the parks.
These words of secretary Lane, set down almost 40 years ago, could not be improved upon in describing our own approach to the administration of the national parks of Canada. In meeting day to day problems and in planning future developments we must never lose sight of the ideal. To leave the parks in an absolutely natural state would mean that they could be used by very few people. We must have some man-made improvements but no more at any time than are necessary to make the parks accessible and to meet the needs of visitors in their enjoyment of the parks.
The most difficult problem, therefore, in national parks administration is to preserve at all times the best possible balance between visitors' needs and the preservation of the unspoiled beauties they come to see and enjoy. In achieving this balance there are four rules of the utmost importance that we endeavour to follow with the greatest care. 1. Impairments of the parks must be accepted if without them the average Canadian could not get into the parks, stay in them and reach the natural features that are there for him to enjoy. 2. An impairment for that purpose should not be incurred if it is very serious and if the added benefit in enjoyment of the park is not substantial. 3. All impairments should be regulated and controlled so that they are as small and as few as possible. 4. No impairment should be permitted if its purpose is to provide an enjoyment that can equally well be achieved elsewhere unless that impairment contributes towards or promotes the enjoyment of outdoor recreation in keeping with the purposes for which the parks are established.
Because the parks are preserved for the people of Canada as a whole for very special purposes, not for the inhabitants of one area

but for the people of Canada as a whole, it follows that special groups and interests do not have within the parks all the rights and privileges that may be theirs in other parts of the country. To maintain areas in a special way requires special rules and regulations which in other places would be quite unnecessary. When we realize that the government of all community life across the country is based primarily on the needs and wishes of the local people and is conditioned by a desire to stimulate their commercial and industrial life to their greater gain and higher living standard, we can appreciate that, without special regulations, the natural beauties of the parks would be destroyed within a very few years.
We have seen countryside ruined by billboards. We have seen ugly industrial buildings erected in areas that formerly were beautiful. We have all seen these things, and in most areas we have to accept them as part of our normal way of life, but is there anyone among us who has not thought of this occasionally with regret?
In the national parks we have the priceless opportunity to avoid all this and to preserve some of the most beautiful parts of Canada for all time for all the people. To this end, the National Parks Act and regulations made thereunder are designed, and the government of Canada is charged with an important responsibility. Our regulations must meet the needs now and in the future of a nationwide park system. There are basic management requirements common to all the parks and our approach to these must always be the same. To give special treatment in one place would lead to special treatment in another, and the national character of the system would be lost. For this reason, decisions have to be taken nationally here in Ottawa, in spite of the criticism that we hear at times from the local people. These decisions have to be taken on a nation-wide basis because they could affect more than one park and some of the cases have to be handled with great care.
Moreover, we have to consider the effect of our decisions on conditions that will exist 50, 100 or even more years in the future, and this is an administrative problem that is rarely appreciated. If at times our reaction in the department to changing times and modern innovations may be slow, there are, I am sure, few thoughtful persons who would wish us to make hasty decisions and in so doing endanger the heritage of Canada's future.
But, Mr. Chairman, what are these daily problems that we face? Many of our problems lie in trying to give the best possible service to a steadily increasing number of visitors with a limited budget. These are
Supply-Northern Affairs met without too much difficulty, and I can say with certainty that the vast majority of visitors to our parks have returned home well satisfied, to the credit of our dedicated staffs in the field and often as well to the credit of conscientious private operators of cabins, hotels, motels, restaurants and other concessions within the parks.
The most continuing problems that we face and the most criticisms that we receive arise from the desire of various persons to do things, to build things or to regulate things within the parks for their own personal or local benefit. Even the minister is in danger when he says "No" of being branded as a bureaucrat. There is a tendency for some people to imply that we make regulations for the fun of making regulations. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there is nothing that is less fun than the making of regulations. What we are doing we are doing honestly and conscientiously in order to try to protect the serious purposes that are basic in the parks.
When a person wishes to erect a large advertising sign and we say no we are told that we are standing in the way of business development. Would hon. members like to see billboards in our parks? I doubt it. There is room enough outside, as a matter of fact. I am sorry that the hon. member for Bow River is not here; because I should like him to hear this. When a person wishes to take up permanent residence in a park, to retire there, even though his presence is not required to serve the needs of visitors, and we say "no", we are told that we are interfering with personal freedom.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was not complaining about his absence. I was just saying that I was sorry he was not here. I am sorry to hear that he is ill.
I am sure that hon. members can figure out for themselves what would happen if a private citizen demanded public land in a municipal park-or, let us say, in any park in Canada-for his private home. It comes to exactly the same thing.
When it becomes necessary, in view of the greatly increased numbers of visitors, to rearrange camp grounds or to restrict their use to the period of a normal holiday, and when in the course of these changes certain persons lose some of the privileges they have enjoyed in the past-such as that of

Supply-Northern Affairs occupying the best place in the camp grounds over a whole season-we are told that we are depriving people of their rights, and our decisions can be most unpopular among the groups concerned.
We do our best to meet particular interests when this can be done without prejudice to all the people of Canada; but once a situation becomes such that the interest of the people as a whole is suffering or is likely to suffer in future, we are duty bound to all Canadians-to whom the parks belong-to make the best arrangements possible.
There is a special problem in some of the parks, namely that of the townsites. I should like to say a few words about that matter. There are major townsites at Banff and Jasper and there are smaller townsites in a number of other parks. There is a tendency for those businesses serving visitors to concentrate at one point within a park, and as tourist volume increases these town-sites grow in size. A large proportion of our problems in administering the parks arise out of the townsites. They have many of the aspects of municipalities across Canada and there must be regulations to control their orderly development.
Outside the parks, municipal control is in the hands of the local people and is exercised through their elected representatives. The driving force in this control is naturally the economic betterment of the particular community, and the people there do not have to worry about the effects of their actions on other communities across Canada, or even to any great extent about the effects on visitors except from the standpoint of potential business. All of this is right and proper, as the community exists to meet the needs of the local people.
In the park townsites, however, the situation is totally different. The communities are in themselves an impairment of the natural state of the park, and can be permitted under the Parks Act only because they are required to meet the needs of visitors. That is their only reason for existing. For this reason, the development of park town-sites must be governed from the point of view of the needs of visitors to the parks- those of the present and those of fifty or even one hundred years from now-and not of the needs of those whose interest in the parks is commercial operation in one form or another.
In administering the townsites we endeavour to create an economic atmosphere within which sufficient businesses to meet genuine tourist needs may reasonably prosper; and to some extent, therefore, regulations must
[Mr. Lesage.l

take into account the needs of these businesses. Their needs, however, must always be judged in the light of the interest of all Canadians now and in the future in having the parks preserved for their benefit, and their right in that connection. The preservation of the parks is the essential object and at the same time, the limiting factor not the requirements of any particular business that is or would like to be within a park.
While residents and businesses in the park townsites do not have the same control of their local affairs that would be the case outside the parks, they do have the opportunity through their local representatives to present to the park administration their problems and needs. An example of this is the Banff advisory council, and at the present time one is being formed in Jasper. As far as possible, the wishes of these local representatives are met; and when this cannot be done we always endeavour to give full explanation of all our actions. Sometimes, of course, there simply are not funds available; at other times local wishes run counter to the principles on which the parks are founded and there is no choice but to withold consent.
While local people in the townsites do not have the normal control over the operation and development of their communities, they also do not have to bear the normal tax load. Townsite residents are charged nothing for construction and maintenance of streets, for snow removal, for police services, for public park areas or for administration costs. They contribute generally less than half the cost of the installation and maintenance of water, sewer and fire protection systems wherever these are provided. A resident of Banff townsite, with a property assessment of $6,000 would pay tax of about $107 per year, including school and hospital taxes. The average tax on similar property in three towns of comparable size in Alberta would be over $300. One may compare $107 with $300.
For a typical business site with an assessment of about $13,000 in Banff, the tax would be about $225. In the other three towns in Alberta which I have mentioned, it would be over $750 or more than three times as much. If townsite residents in the parks were to find themselves located outside the parks tomorrow, they would be faced with a tremendous added financial burden, even if an outright gift were made to them of the extensive capital works that have been installed almost entirely from taxes paid by Canadians as a whole.
Before I resume my seat, may I say this. We might ask ourselves what we are doing about the future of the parks. The most

immediate need is for better road facilities. A major increase is provided-as I mentioned on July 12-for this purpose in the 1956-57 estimates. This is part of an 8-year program completely to reconstruct all major park highways and bring them to adequate standards. The cost, apart from the trans-Canada highway across Banff and Yoho parks, will probably exceed $60 million. During this same 8-year period, while a large portion of funds made available by parliament will be devoted to highways, it is proposed to continue with the present major program of improvement and extension of park facilities used by the public, including camp grounds and picnic areas, comfort stations, bathing beach developments, and many others. Improvements and extensions will also be made in facilities required by the department for the better maintenance and operation of the parks.
Work is now proceeding on the establishment of a special planning group within the parks branch of the department which will be charged with the task of gathering data and working out and recommending long-range plans for the development of all the parks so that this development may proceed in an orderly manner and in keeping with the anticipated steady increase in the number of visitors over the years. I have outlined at some length our approach to national park management and development. I hope this will help all those who are interested in understanding our problems and the way in which we endeavour to solve them. Canada receives many benefits from the parks, such as increased tourist business, a livelihood for those catering to the tourist industry and the provision of work for many hundreds in the operation of the park. Above all, Canadians receive those intangible benefits of quiet relaxation and recreation in our priceless areas of peace and grandeur. The preservation of this heritage and placing it within easier reach of the people of Canada is the constant aim that I have, together with the officials of the department.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister has just given us a considerable discourse on national parks inspired, I have no doubt, by the fact that there has been a great deal of criticism of the administration of the parks, particularly in Alberta where the two largest parks are situated. Quite a lot of the minister's speech was taken up with the basic conceptions which were in mind when the national parks were formed, and with those I must say that I agree, on the whole, as I think does nearly everyone in the country. The minister also took up quite a bit of time I thought in setting up straw men and knocking them down.
Supply-Northern Affairs He took up some time also in making analogies which were not applicable in point of fact. I am not going to deal with all those points in detail at this time, as I think perhaps the criticisms which I have to make of the administration of the national parks might perhaps be more appropriate when we come to deal specifically with the national parks branch.
I would just comment on one of the points the minister made shortly before he sat down and of which he seemed to make a great deal. It was that taxes are a great deal less in Banff than they are in comparable towns. The fact still remains, Mr. Chairman, that there exists in Banff and Jasper, as well as any other town sites which may exist in national parks, taxation without representation.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: They are not taxes, they are service charges.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to remind the minister that the tea tax which provoked the Boston tea party was a very small tax, in fact it was only a token tax, but it gave rise to the American revolution. I think the minister, by trying to make a big point of the fact that taxes are less in Banff than in places of comparable size outside national parks, is batting on a very sticky wicket indeed.
I should like to deal somewhat generally with some of the phases of this department which, of course, consists of five more or less non-related branches. There is the northern administration of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon; national parks; water resources; the forestry branch and the travel bureau. There is very little connection between most of these branches, and therefore I will touch on some of them in a general way at this time and leave what we may call the detailed criticism and questions until we come to the specific items. I think perhaps that is a more orderly way of conducting a discussion.
The government administration and development of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon territories is probably the most important matter to come under this department, at least from the long-term development of Canada as a great nation. At the present time there is much more interest directed to our northland than used to be the case. There is a variety of reasons why this should be so. First of all, our other frontiers have disappeared and this is the only great frontier left. Naturally, people who are interested in new things and new developments have had their attention directed to the north. Then, the great improvement which has taken place in

Supply-Northern Affairs transportation, especially air transportation, has made the north much more accessible than it was before. This has made it possible for a greatly increased number of people to go into the north country, carry on developments there and see what the prospects were.
Then, there have been some considerable mineral discoveries which, of course, have excited a good deal of interest and have taken a considerable number of people into our north country; especially has this been true so far as uranium is concerned. Of course, there has been quite a bit of gold prospecting and development of gold mines in this territory. However, I think the greatest factor in opening up the north and increasing the interest of the people in it has been defence requirements. The string of radar stations now being constructed to constitute the D.E.W. line will, of course, be permanent establishments right across the Arctic. The supplying of these D.E.W. line stations means constant and regular transportation to areas of the far north in which no white man, or very few, had ever been up to a very short time ago.
Now, in connection with the establishment of the D.E.W. line, it seems to me that the Canadian government has not been sufficiently in evidence-in fact, it has not even been represented at all in some of the places where development is occurring in that area. In that connection I should like to read a few excerpts from an article which appeared in Maclean's magazine of May 26, written by Ralph Allen. The article is entitled, "Will D.E.W. line cost Canada its Northland?" I should like to read a few excerpts from this to indicate to the committee what the situation in the north was found to be by a very experienced writer. Talking of the D.E.W. line he said:
It is the charter under which a tenth of Canada may very well become the world's most northerly banana republic. For a sum of money that has been officially estimated at $400 million we have at least temporarily traded off our whole northern frontier. In law. we still own this northern frontier. In fact we do not.
I am not going into the military end of this at all. I am going to deal with it entirely from the point of view of northern affairs because the minister's department is responsible for administering northern affairs and for maintaining Canadian law and order in that area, maintaining our sovereignty over it. Therefore, the problem can really be placed squarely on the doorstep of the minister.
Another excerpt from this article reads:
The suggestion that Canada is only the nominal ruler of this important part of Canada and that the United States is the real ruler is not taken

seriously anywhere except on the D.E.W. line itself. There the truth is palpable and inescapable.
Now, I am not saying that Mr. Allen was the only newspaper reporter who went on the trip. There was a considerable number of United States and Canadian newsmen and all the articles I have seen written by Canadian newsmen were along the same lines as this article by Mr. Allen.
Another excerpt:
The significant point, it seems to me, is that in this single area alone-the whole vexed and tortured area of security-there lie the seeds of serious discord and possible further encroachments on Canada's control of the Canadian north.
I should like to emphasize that last phrase, "possible further encouragement on Canada's control of the Canadian north". Well, it is the job of this department to assure that this encroachment does not take place.
I have one final excerpt:
The most experienced and responsible Canadian I met in the north was a man I'd rather not identify more closely than that. I asked him bluntly:	"Do you and your friends resent the
presence of the Americans here?" "No", he said sadly, "It's the other way around. They resent our presence here".
I think that that article and articles by other people who were on this trip have caused a considerable number of Canadians to think pretty seriously about what our situation is in the north, the extent to which our control of that area still remains in our hands, the extent to which it has been lost and particularly what steps should be taken by our defence department, yes, but by this department particularly, to ensure that Canadian control of that area continues, is not further impaired and, as a mattter of fact, is restored.
There was an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal in April on this same matter, and it gives some suggestions as to what might be done by this department in order to correct the situation which was found by the newsmen who went up to the north. I should like to read part of it: It reads:
It is not sufficient to proclaim a right and then walk away and forget it. There is need of official Canadian representation at every D.E.W. line site where more than a few men are stationed, a continuing reminder that the final authority is not the construction or operations superintendent but the government of Canada.
And the situation as found by these newsmen was that the final authority-in fact, practically the only authority at these various D.E.W. line stations-was the senior operations man present, who was an American. The editorial continues:
The representative may be a mounted policeman or northern service officer of the northern affairs department. It is essential that he be there

to see that Canadian laws and regulations-and if necessary Canadian dignities-are observed and it will be poor economy if the government thinks that this task can be done adequately by sporadic visits by policemen and service officers.
The present understanding is that there will be a man from the R.C.M.P. or other representative at every main site on the line when it is in operation within the next two years. There are also to be auxiliary and intermediate sites where it may be assumed there will be smaller groups of employees. In this ice-bound land each of these isolated units must be thought of as an island to which will come voyageurs of the air, some of whom will be from the United States with no landing until they reach their northern destination.
None should be left in any doubt, no matter how new Canada and the Arctic may be to him, that this is Canadian soil. This requires the Canadian ensign be given pride of place in displays of flags. It requires too that there be an agent of the Canadian civil power on hand to see the formalities of immigration, customs, game laws, and all the rest, are properly observed.
No citizen of the United States will object to such an arrangement but if Canada fails to see it is provided she invites embarrassment.
This is a matter which I would like the minister, when he speaks later when we get to this particular item of the Northwest Territories, to say something about, and it is a matter on which I hope there will be some immediate action taken, and that it will be provided that there will be a northern service officer or a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at each of these stations, not only at a few of the main stations. The cost would not be very great, and I think the significance of it, and the effect it would have, would be far out of proportion to the relatively small cost which would be involved.
I should like to say something about the resources of our north country. They are, of course, much greater than was thought up to only a few years ago. As a matter of fact, until quite recently the north was considered only as a great non-productive waste, mostly rock and barren lands. We now know that there are great mineral deposits there. I have already mentioned uranium and gold, but there is, of course, one of the greatest lead-zinc deposits at Pine Point which has ever been discovered and one which makes it quite likely that a railroad will be, and could profitably be, built into that area. There is water power there to be developed. Some has been developed already to a limited extent. There is a field at Fort Norman which has been under development for some time and, of course, the whole valley of the Mackenzie river is potential oil and gas land, and undoubtedly a good deal of oil and gas will be discovered and produced in that area.
There is a considerable amount of forest cover in the Mackenzie river area, particularly the western Arctic area, and on the
Supply-Northern Affairs basis of that undoubtedly a considerable amount of timber will be cut, and there is the possibility of a paper mill or paper mills in this area.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The Slave river.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is the Mackenzie river valley. When I speak of the Mackenzie river valley I mean the Mackenzie and rivers running into it. It is all the Mackenzie river valley or system.
There is also, of course, the possibility of a certain amount of agriculture, sufficient, at any rate, to supply the local inhabitants living up there with vegetables, dairy products and things of that sort.
Fishing in the lakes is already a considerable industry and will, no doubt, be expanded. And then, of course, there is what was the original only wealth of the country, namely, the fur industry, which unfortunately has now declined very considerably. However, rather than being a great non-productive waste, we now know this north country is rich in resources, capable of supporting quite a considerable population and capable of sending down materials to the rest of Canada which will support a great many more. In other words, we have a great area there which is well worth developing. Unfortunately, the development has been very slow in coming.
Transportation, of course, is the most important thing in order to develop our north country. The department now seems to be much more aware of this than they were even a year ago. When the estimates of this department were before the estimates committee last year we spent quite a bit of time, and a number of us placed a great deal of emphasis on the development of roads, waterways and air transport and the building of a railway. At that time the minister was rather discouraging in the remarks that he made to us and more or less gave the impression that this was fairly fanciful; it was quite a long way in the future, and so on. As I say, since then apparently there has been a change of heart and the department now seems to be more aware of the need of developing transportation, and developing it immediately, and not waiting until some long period in the future. I was greatly cheered by the brief entitled "The Northwest Territories-Its Economic Prospects" which was presented to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects by R. G. Robertson, commissioner of the Northwest

Supply-Northern Affairs Territories and deputy minister of the department. On page 19 of this brief I find the following:
.	.	. any program designed to stimulate the
economic development of the territories must begin with a determined attack on the problem of transportation.
There is absolutely no question about that. I am glad the department has now recognized this fact and I am particularly glad that it envisages something more extensive being done than was the case a year ago. On page 23 of the brief the following appears:
The most important element, however, is a whole set of high costs due, directly and indirectly, to problems of transportation. These costs can all be brought down substantially.
That is one of the things we harped on last year and from the brief I gather that the department is now working on this question, I hope vigorously. The paragraph continues:
Nothing else will have so great an effect in stimulating economic development.
On page 24 and subsequent pages the brief refers to the building of the railroad to Pine Point. We spoke about this at some length last year. I will read just a brief section concerning this subject:
.	.	. three methods by which transportation
facilities into the Northwest Terrtiories might be improved. The first is the construction of a railroad to Great Slave lake. The second is construction of roads into promising resource development areas when and as indications suggest that these areas, given highway transportation, would be economic to develop. The third is the adoption of the policy of supplying the newly constructed defence stations in the Northwest Territories by commercial air services and the establishment of a network of scheduled commercial airlines in the Arctic.
I would really have liked to take up considerably more time dealing with transportation in the north and what might be done to improve it and I would particularly like to have referred at greater length to the projected railway to Pine Point; however, I will leave the subject of transportation at this point and merely ask the minister when he speaks if he will tell us how far along the plans are for this railway, if anything concrete has been arrived at and when construction may be expected to begin.
The problem of the native population is, of course, one of the greatest problems in the Northwest Territories. The old means of livelihood such as trapping for fur and fishing, particularly the former, are rapidly disappearing. I understand that the cariboo have been disappearing and have been killed off at a fairly rapid rate. The cariboo constituted the bulk of the food of a considerable proportion

of the northern population and something has to be substituted in its place.
Some of the Eskimos and others in the north are securing employment on the construction of the D.E.W. line which, of course, serves to accustom them to our way of life. As a result of accustoming them to our way of life it perhaps makes it difficult for them to return to their old way of life. What to do with the native population of the north, how most usefully to employ them, how to keep them fed and particularly how to put them in the position of being able to feed themselves are some of the chief problems in the whole matter of administration of the north.
The department concerned puts out what is called a northern affairs bulletin. I have in my hand a copy of the June-July 1956 bulletin and dealing with the subject of education it says:
. . . every effort is being made to provide adult education of a type which will equip all ablebodied men to take on jobs which will result in a higher level of economy and standard of living throughout this vast area.
I am in very great sympathy with the idea of training men in the north to take on jobs but after this has been accomplished the main thing is the provision of jobs. It is of little use to train an Eskimo to be a machinist, we will say, if there is nothing to which he can apply his trade. I realize that the problem is an extremely difficult one and I would like the minister to give us at least some indication of what is being done to meet this problem.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Before we took dinner recess I had just been mentioning the fact that in my opinion the system of tendering and letting of contracts in this department leaves much to be desired and that the old patronage system is operating here perhaps to a greater extent than in any other department in the government.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask a question?

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, I only have seven minutes left to me now and I do want to finish what I have to say. I shall be glad to answer any questions as soon as I have finished.
In connection with this matter, to begin with, there is not a free system of tendering, as far as I am aware, in regard to quite a number of items which are secured by this department. The only people who are allowed to tender are those who are on a preferred list. People who are not on that list do not even get an invitation to tender. In other words, the tenders are not advertised
Supply-Northern Affairs in the newspapers as they are in other departments, and only those political friends of the government who happen to be on that particular list get an opportunity to tender at all.
When a tender is put in, whether it is on that basis or whether it is on the basis of an open tender, the unsuccessful tenderer is not told who has got the contract or the price at which he has got it. In the Department of Defence Production, on the contrary, for example, if an unsuccessful tenderer sends in a stamped addressed envelope he can return a form which they actually give to him, and he will be sent the name of the successful tenderer and the price at which the tender was let. In this particular department, if a man asks for the name of a tenderer and the price at which it was let, they send him back a letter saying, "It is not the policy of this department to divulge prices or suppliers." In other words, the whole thing is kept under a veil of secrecy, and the people who have tendered have no means of knowing who got the contract. Perhaps they can send people to investigate and find out eventually, but they are not told and have no means of finding out what the price is.
I have just referred to what is done in the Department of Defence Production. It is quite plain that the method of tendering in that department is very much better than what prevails in this department as far as the public interest is concerned. A man sends in and he gets back the name of the successful tenderer and the price at which the contract is let. I am glad that the Minister of Defence Production is coming in, as I am holding up his department, as a model for the one that is under discussion in this particular case. As a matter of fact, the method used in the Department of Defence Production is a very much better system, as far as the public interest is concerned. The unsuccessful tenderer then can see at what price the contract was let, and the next time a tender is advertised and he puts in a bid for it, he is naturally going to sharpen up his pencil and put in as good a price as he can. As a result, the government and the people of Canada are going to get the contract filled in most cases at a better price than they would if this policy of secrecy and refusal to give prices existed as it does in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.

You can cut down forests and it takes a good many years before they will reproduce themselves. Then we have water power, another important national resource and one which we must utilize to the fullest extent. Along with our water power we must consider our non-reproducing natural resources such as coal and similar minerals.
I am going to subdivide our water resources into two parts. First of all, I should like to refer to the water resources found in the natural flow of our rivers, and I am going to refer specifically to the province of Nova Scotia. Here I should like to say that in my opinion the development of hydro power on our non-tidal rivers in Nova Scotia is most uneconomical because in order to provide the necessary storage basins and a level flow of water throughout the year it is necessary to flood such large areas of the river basins that the natural growth in those basins, whether agricultural or forest, is destroyed, and the initial cost of such a development is not a true picture of the actual cost to the economy of the country. In other words, we should consider when we flood such tremendous areas of our province what the potential production of those areas would have been in future years and add that to the cost of the development.
We do have one great source of power in our province which I believe has never been actually explored to the hilt. It is true that an investigation was made, and there is one going on now, of Passamaquoddy bay to see just what we could do to develop power from the tides of the bay of Fundy. A few years ago an investigation was also made on the Petitcodiac and the Memramcook rivers, in New Brunswick. They have been going out and coming in ever since mankind was created and they will go out and come in just as long as humanity exists.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on the first item in these estimates in order to impress upon the minister the importance of taking early and effective action to bring into the northern territories the one very important thing that will surely contribute to the development of that great country. Before I say what I have to say on that matter, I should like to comment just briefly on the statement of the minister this afternoon in connection with our national parks. These playgrounds of Canada come under the supervision of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I listened very attentively to the statement he made and 1 found myself in almost complete agreement with his policy as he expressed it this afternoon. I was born and raised right close to one of these great national parks. For many years I have been somewhat concerned about the future policy in respect of them. More particularly I have wondered whether we might get into the same frame of mind as have people in the United States where the national parks have become commercialized and it is difficult for people to find rest and relaxation and the enjoyment of beautiful and natural things such as we have been able to find in our parks in this country. So I was gratified when he said it will be the continued policy of the department to operate the parks in such a manner that for many years to come they will be unspoiled, that the natural beauty will be retained. I took for granted from what he said that commercialism in these parks will be restrained just as far as it possibly can be. I commend the minister for that attitude because there are so many of us who would like to see these parks remain in perpetuity, if possible, unspoiled by the commercial hand of man.
I hope it will be possible for us to induce the building of sufficient facilities so that tourists will be able to come from far and 67509-438
Supply-Northern Affairs near to enjoy our natural beauties with us. I am convinced that in our national parks in Canada we have the most beautiful playground in the world, without any question. I have travelled over much of the world and 1 think that I have never seen anything to equal the beauties that we have in Banff, Jasper and Waterton national parks in Alberta. I am only naming those that are in my own province but there are others, also. I will support the minister 100 per cent in the expressed policy that he brought before the committee this afternoon.
Now, I should like to say just a word about the northern territories that the minister has visited on several occasions. I am glad to see that he has familiarized himself with the territory. I was very happy when the minister furnished me with a copy of the brief that was submitted to the royal commission on economic affairs by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories. I read what Mr. Robertson had to say about the development of that vast north country. Anyone reading the report and studying the maps and other facts that are obtainable about the north country cannot help but be convinced that the northern territories have a very great part to play in the future in the building of a strong and secure Canada. When we think of the recent developments in the area, what those who have been prospecting throughout the country have found, the evidence of great natural mineral wealth, I am sure that we cannot escape the conclusion that the earliest possible development of this territory would be desirable in the interests of a strong Canada.
I am not only interested in the northern territories from the point of view of having their development assured in the near future for building a strong Canada, which is of course our paramount consideration, but I am also interested because the development of the northern territories is so closely bound up with the development of my own area, the Peace river country. So I speak just briefly at this time in support of what Mr. Robertson has so well pointed out in his brief. I do not intend to read it at all, but merely refer to it in a general way. He has taken the position that the most important thing is transportation. I agree with him wholeheartedly. I will go further and say that the northern territories cannot contribute what they can possibly contribute to the strength and security of Canada until we do have adequate transportation. Further than that, I am satisfied that we cannot see the possibility of the early development of the resources of the great north country until we have rail transportation.

Supply-Northern Affairs
We can talk about water transportation and air transportation from now until doomsday, but it will not solve the problem of the area for the simple reason that water transportation into the northern territory is possible only during a short part of the year and it becomes exceedingly costly at other times. Air transportation is always expensive. There are only two ways of getting into the northern territories today by the water and land route. One way is through Fort Smith and the other way is through Hay River, which is a settlement on the Great Slave lake.
Now, the Fort Smith route starts from Waterways, the railhead, and is not a good possible route for the reason that you have a long portage and the costs are too great. Not only that, but the river and lake freeze over very early in the fall, making it impossible to carry on transportation beyond the latter part of September, usually. The other route by which you can enter the great northern territories by land and water is through Grimshaw, the railhead in the Peace river country, and down the Mackenzie highway into Great Slave lake by way of the settlement at Hay River. Now, that distance from Grimshaw on the Northern Alberta Railways to Hay River on the Great Slave lake is about 381 miles, almost the same distance as it would be from here to London, Ontario. This gives some idea of the tremendous distance. The route down the Mackenzie highway is an easy gradient. It is not a difficult one through which to build a rail route at all. Much of the clearing has been done along that route and every few miles one finds a very fine farming area which, when it reaches its full development, will contribute immeasurably to the support of a railway to cover that 381 mile distance.
Mr. Robertson quite correctly points out in his brief that if we had a rail route approximately 400 miles closer to the Mackenzie valley than it is now, which would be possible if we were to extend the Northern Alberta Railways from Grimshaw to Hay River, the rates would be cut down to the point where the working of the ore bodies that have been recently discovered at Pine Point would become quite possible and competitive. Now, that is an important point because we know that there are at least 60 million tons of high grade lead and zinc ore in that area that can be mined very largely by the open cut method. If we had the rail transportation to carry that ore out, then the mines would become competitive and that ore bed would contribute to Canada's strength because one of the things we do need is new sources of base metal.
There is one just across the borderline from the northern part of Alberta and along the southern shore of Great Slave lake fifty miles or so east of Hay River settlement.
I point these things out merely to emphasize the need for early action to get that rail connection from the Peace river territory into that area to make transportation possible the year round; to make it possible for these mines and ore bodies to be worked on a competitive basis. Not only that, but I am satisfied it would help open up vast areas of fine farm territory which would contribute to the support of the railway in the years to come. I am sure the minister agrees with me when I say that in times past transportation has preceded intensive development rather than following it. I am quite sure that he must agree with me when I say that in the early days of Canada the railways did not wait to see the development well on its way before they started building railroads. They had some pioneering spirit in those days.
Today it appears the railways do not want to move unless they see an assured immediate return from freight haulage that will make it possible for them to pay their full expenses from the beginning. I do not think that is the spirit at all, and I am certain-the minister I believe will agree with me-he will if he thinks upon it-that if the Northern Alberta Railways were not operated under a joint ownership, if there were more competition up there a rail line would be built into the Northwest Territories very early. I believe that the northern areas would have rail transportation much sooner if the Canadian National Railways owned and operated the Northern Alberta Railways by themselves. The Canadian Pacific Railway, of course, because of the fact that it is deeply interested in the Pine Point ore bed through the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company which owns, I think, the greater portion of the mineral rights there, will continue to stay in the area just as long as it possibly can. It may never get out. But I do believe that the minister, if he will put pressure on his colleague, the Minister of Transport, and others of his colleagues, could succeed in getting a railhead 400 miles farther down in the Mackenzie area than it is now, and he could get that soon.
I know the argument has often been raised -and I believe the railroads have said this recently-that if the government of Canada were to subsidize the full cost of the building of the road at the present time there would not be enough tonnage hauled over the railroad from Grimshaw to Hay River to pay the costs. Well, I am not so sure of that. I should like to see more figures. That may

have been true a few years ago, but I remind the minister that every few miles along that route down the Mackenzie highway farming areas have been opened up that are now producing very large quantities of grain and livestock and lumber. I remind the minister that those areas are being extended. The Alberta government is opening up very large tracts of land for settlement. They are offering it on a homestead basis to young men who wish to establish themselves in farming and for a $10 registration fee they are able to get 320 acres of that land for development, and it is going fast. The area is building up rapidly and within a few years, if transportation were provided, the tonnage of agricultural products coming out of that country would be a surprise to everybody because it is good country; it is productive, and the change that has taken place on the face of that land in the past four or five years is amazing to anybody who has seen it.
This is completely apart from what is being found in the northern territories, and I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say this: add the potential ore development, the potential oil development, the other developments in the north to the farming possibilities in the northern Peace river country and you can make a very fine case for the early building of a rail line from Grim-shaw into Great Slave lake. Therefore, I urge the minister to use every energy that he possesses to get that development. He should talk sternly and earnestly to his colleague, the Minister of Transport, and to the railways. We will back him, and we certainly do not want to do anything to make it difficult for him to talk. We want him to know that we are supporting him and, certainly, the policy which was outlined by him this afternoon and by the commissioner of the northern territories, Mr. Robertson, as we find it in his brief to the royal commission.
