Mr. Chairman, because the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Calgary North dealt with several of the matters which I had intended to bring to the attention of the minister I will attempt to save the time of the committee by not repeating some of the things that have already been said. Therefore, in the few minutes at my disposal I shall confine my remarks to a few general observations on one or two other aspects of the minister's department. I think everyone agrees that the prosperity of Canada at the present time depends very largely on our oil and mineral resources. The continued expansion of those resources will bring greater returns to the economy of this country, and therefore we can say that Canada's north holds the key 67509-438J
Supply-Northern Affairs to Canada's future economic prosperity in so far as it depends on our oil and mineral resources.
Someone said a while ago that the potentialities of Canada's north are tremendous. I would suggest-and I think everyone would agree, including the minister-that at the present time we are unacquainted with those potentialities. Certainly, the expansion and the development that have taken place in our north country have been very spectacular. Spectacular as that development may be, it must be remembered that little or nothing was done prior to the outbreak of world war II. For that reason, and because of recent happenings in the north, the developments have been somewhat of a spectacular nature. However, it seems to me the problem we are confronted with today is to see that there is a successful and orderly development of our north country.
I am sure that those of us who have had an opportunity-and the minister will agree with this, too-of flying over our Canadian north could not help being impressed with that vast land, its sparse population and the over-all inhospitality of the country. Certainly, it would be a bold and irresponsible person who would suggest that to develop the Canadian north does not present apparently almost insurmountable problems. However, we have to tackle the problem. The pattern of development must be such that the wealth that is created accrues to the people of Canada; and secondly, and possibly more important still, we must see to it that the social aspects of the native people are protected in order that there is the least possible dislocation so that those people might be integrated into the kind of life that they are going to have to come in contact with if they are going to survive and get for themselves the kind of welfare that is necessary. It is to be hoped that we shall not repeat the blunders and do the things that we have done in the past with regard to this very important problem of seeing to it that the native people of the north are given a fair break, a chance to retain their dignity and to get for themselves the kind of economic security that is so necessary.
Mr. Chairman, this problem of the native people seems to me to have been uppermost in the minds of the commissioners of the Northwest Territories when they presented their brief to the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects last fall, for these commissioners pointed out in many instances the great necessity for the immediate development of the mineral and oil resources of Canada's north in order to make it possible for the native population to survive. They point out that because of the

Supply-Northern Affairs health Services that have been given to these people over the past few years the population has increased and the effect has been that the game resources are almost depleted.
As those of us who have had anything to do with Indians are aware-I am not acquainted with Eskimos but I presume they would have the same characteristics-native people are not conservation-minded. Because of this the game resources upon which these people rely for their welfare have become depleted. We now have the situation where the native people are depending more and more upon commercial food supplies. Because of the fact that fur prices have declined and deteriorated substantially over the last two or three years the native now finds himself in a very precarious position. With the money he receives from his furs he is not able to buy enough food to maintain his health.
I wish to refer to the report made by Mr. Gordon Robertson, one of the commissioners, when he was giving evidence before the Gordon commission. He said that:
The Indian population had to live on sub-1933 incomes while paying 1956 prices plus high freight charges.
The result of what has taken place is that the natives are moving to the settlements and are accepting seasonal employment whenever it is available. They are recipients not only of the family allowance but also relief payments.
It has been suggested that relief payments should be increased and one suggestion is that they should be doubled. I think that would be disastrous because the recipients of large amounts of relief soon become economic derelicts. They lose their selfrespect and it automatically follows that they lose their place in society; and when the day comes when economic opportunities are made available for these people they will not be able to fit in nor grasp them because of their dependency on relief payments.
In the interim I think it is important to maintain their natural way of life. I think we will have to do that for some time to come until the day arrives when integration will be possible. This will facilitate an orderly and natural adjustment to a new way of life. I think the government is going to be forced to undertake a conservation program to conserve not only the fur but the game in that area in order that these people will have some source of income in the intervening period which they must face.
Along with the recommendations made by the Northwest Territories council I would also suggest that the government give serious consideration to supporting the price of fur.

I realize that this presents a genuine problem and I believe the commissioners who are close to the situation realize this, too. However, surely it is not an insurmountable problem; surely a solution can be found. I can foresee that there might be some abuses and some bootlegging might take place although supporting the price of fur would be comparatively costly. I wonder if we can afford not to do this. I would strongly suggest that this should be given serious consideration by the government in the interim period these people are going to experience.
I believe, too, it would be feasible for the government to establish trading stores in the north. We have established trading stores in the province of Saskatchewan and they have been of great benefit to the native population. It would appear to me that this would do away with many of the questionable practices that are carried on by the occasional free trader and also by the Hudson's Bay Company.
I recall being in a trading store in the comparatively far north not long ago and seeing on the shelves rows of canned dog food. I said to the trader, "It looks a little ridiculous to me to see Indians buying prepared dog food in cans and paying the price that would have to be asked for this commodity." I was told that they did not feed it to their dogs but were using it as the basic ingredient to make home brew. I think we have here a glaring example of the exploitation of these native people by unscrupulous operators. I would strongly suggest to the minister that he give consideration to the establishment of trading stores that would have the interests of the natives at heart.
I would also suggest that the government should undertake a program of providing free air transportation and other free facilities to native people in order that they may go out prospecting for minerals. I believe these people could do an excellent job in this regard. They have become perfectly adapted to the country and the climate and I am sure this would be one means of providing extremely profitable and suitable employment for them.
Concerning the question of education, while I agree that under some circumstances residential schools perhaps cannot be avoided I would suggest that wherever possible the government should establish day schools in preference to residential schools. I urge that there should be the closest co-operation between the officials of the Northwest Territories council and the minister's department in selecting a curriculum.

I was glad to learn this afternoon that the minister is co-operating with the council and that the curriculum being drawn up is emphasizing various skills that will be of some practical value to the native people rather than more academic subjects.
I also suggest there will have to be a revision of salaries for school teachers going into the north country. I think it is unfortunate that a school teacher going from a province into the territories is not able to have his or her superannuation recognized by the province which he or she has left to go into the territories to take up a teaching job for the minister's department. I know of one or two instances where qualified teachers with a certain dedication went into that country and found out that their superannuation ceased, and they immediately returned to the province which they had left. I think that is unfortunate.

I noticed an item in the press not long ago; I am not going to read it, but it is very critical of the kind of supervision that is being given to these people by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
In conclusion I should like to say that it is the prime interest of the government and the minister who has charge of this department to see to the welfare of our northern native people. We have two resources to develop: our natural resources and our human resources. I am sure that our record in the past has not been too good, but certainly, we can develop and integrate our northern native human resources if we tackle the problem with determination and imagination.

I rise tonight to take part in the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources because of the fact that, whilst the department deals more with northern Ontario, we in western Ontario are very much interested in the department, and I should like to make a few comments on it.
People from the United States are much more inclined to pay attention to their historical background, whilst we Canadians, on the other hand, are probably prone to under-emphasize our historical past. Those of us who pay any attention to history will realize that it is only through the building up of history and traditions that a nation becomes great. It has been said that at the time of the French revolution all the past was cut off and forgotten, and since that time the French nation has never been able to rebuild the traditions of that country as they once were.
Consequently, I am asking that the minister, through the historic sites and monuments board and otherwise, may influence the Canadian people to take a greater interest in our history. While I am dealing with that, I may say that the present chairman of the historic sites and monuments board, Professor Fred Landon of the University of Western Ontario-he	is from London,
Ontario-has done very fine and worthwhile work in that connection. However, whilst that is being done, I do not think that enough is being done. Some encouragement should be given to municipalities to pay some attention to their historical backgrounds. There are a good many societies of one kind and another-I shall mention only the women's institute-that could devote one day or one of their programs to the historical points of interest

Supply-Northern Affairs in the local community. I think there is a very worth-while field for work there.
History does not mean perhaps quite so much to present as to future generations of this country. It is because of that fact that I make this plea tonight. In my county of Middlesex there are now streams on which were situated water mills on which pioneers depended for the processing of their wheat into flour, and many of the people living in those areas are not aware that in those very communities there exist these water mills. I am thinking particularly of the one on the Medway creek, a tributary of the Thames- I am coming to the Thames valley-and that comes under the minister's department. That old mill stream there is almost within the boundaries of the city of London, which has now grown up around it. At one time there was a thriving community at that mill which is now forgotten and which could well be commemorated. It is almost within a stone's throw of the University of Western Ontario.
While we are speaking of historic sites and monuments, I should like to mention that the first minister of agriculture in Sir John Macdonald's government was a Londoner, Sir John Carling, and he established the experimental farm system throughout Canada. The first director of that institution was also one of the illustrious Saunders family of London, Ontario. I think some recognition should be given to the contribution these people have made to the development of Canada, not forgetting Sir Adam Beck, the father of Ontario hydro.
To change the subject for a moment, we are interested in developments thousands of miles from Canada and we spend a lot of money abroad, but at the same time I think we should give some thought to the conservation and use of our resources at home. I am thinking particularly of our water resources. We in western Ontario are very much aware of the scarcity of water at times and yet we are situated in a peninsula almost surrounded by the great lakes. While the minister and I are well aware of the fact that the Ontario water resources committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Snider is doing very worth-while work, the installation of water mains to serve the western Ontario area will be a costly process. As that region is bound to develop industrially and as federal income from that area is also bound to increase with the development of that part of the country, I think it would be wise to develop some plan that would guarantee long-term loans to the municipalities of western Ontario to assist them in the installation of water mains. I feel certain this could be worked out.

On unimpeachable authority I understand that a 12-inch water main could be installed from Ipperwash to London which would serve the many municipalities through which it would pass for some $8 or $9 million.
I also want to point out to the minister that western Ontario and the county of Middlesex particularly were rather disappointed that no provision was made in the estimates for the completion of the dams and water conservation project on the upper Thames river during this year. However, we are satisfied that while it was not included in this year's estimates it is certain that next year will be our turn. I think I should also point out to the minister that it would be wise to complete one river development as far as humanly possible and as quickly as possible in order to have it as a pilot plant, as it were, or pattern from which to gain experience in any future river developments, whether they be in Quebec, the maritimes or the western provinces. When we have gone as far as we have with the development on the Thames it should not take a great deal more to complete it, and then you would have a pilot plant in operation.
Fundamental to soil and water conservation is the development of forest. I think that is one thing about which a lot is said but about which not enough is done, and in my opinion many more submarginal areas than are now used for forest purposes could well be devoted to that use. Unless it is the growing of Christmas trees, it is not likely that any one private individual in western Ontario could plant a forest and expect to reap a harvest from it in his lifetime. Consequently, private individuals are not inclined to go into the reforestation of private land. Therefore I think the future of reforestation must be placed more and more in the hands of river development and conservation authorities if we are going to get the maximum results from forest planting.
I should probably mention here that the forest area in the county of Middlesex is somewhere around 7 per cent, which is about the lowest of any county in the province of Ontario. On the other hand, that only demonstrates how much of the land in the county is suitable for agricultural purposes and has been devoted to that for the last 100 years.
To return to the minister's opening remarks, I was certainly glad to hear him speak in such glowing terms about our national parks throughout Canada. Now is the time to make provision for these parks. As he mentioned, once the development period is over the costs will not be too great and we will have these parks as an investment for future generations for a long time

to come. With the vast area that we have in our country, 1 think we can well afford to have the beauty spots and large areas of Canada as national parks.
Finally, I want to join with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in his plea that the old supreme court building at the foot of the hill be kept as a national monument because of the associations that it has for the people of Canada and its historical association with the fathers of confederation and 1867.	.

Mr. Chairman, I assure you I shall not be long, but I do not want the minister to take it, from the fact that I do not intend to speak for very long, that I do not want him to listen to me. First of all, I should like to say that I appreciate a great deal the co-operation I have had from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and his department in connection with some very vexing problems. I assure him that I appreciate it very much. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Peace River bring to the attention of the house the need for transportation facilities in the area lying north of the Peace river. I should like to call attention to the fact that I believe it is the intention of the British Columbia government to push the Pacific Great Eastern Railway 50 miles farther north to Fort St. John in the Peace river area which is in a direct line toward the Hay river district. I do not know whether or not the route is feasible. I have been told that it is, and it would be a very direct route for trade going to the coast.
In dealing with transportation I would mention again that I should like to see closer co-operation between departments so far as that problem is concerned. I realize that highways are not a problem of the minister unless they are within the parks, but the development of the northern area depends on transportation facilities, air, rail and highway. I would hope that the minister would get together with the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of National Defence and try to work out some way by which at least a portion of the highway between Dawson Creek and Fort St. John could be paved. It is a very important section of the highway that leads to Alaska. The traffic is very heavy and the dust conditions have already caused loss of life in numerous instances.
I should like to make one more point before I sit down. I agree wholeheartedly with the minister in what he has to say about the national parks being for Canadians. However, there are some of our national parks which are astride great passes
Supply-Northern Affairs throughout the Rocky mountains. These parks having been laid out astride these passes in the mountains, it becomes evident that highway traffic for trucks and other commercial vehicles should be allowed to go through. The park with which I am mostly concerned is Jasper park. The total distance from the east boundary to the west boundary is only about 65 miles. I suggest that for 65 miles of highway it would not be amiss if the tourist traffic had roads for it only. Those people that are going to use the park- the Canadian people and others such as Americans-would like to have roads for tourists only. It is only a matter of 65 miles and there is lots of room for other highways, if necessary, to be built from one border to the other of the park and thus allow commercial traffic to pass through this particular area.
I know that the minister has the matter in mind and I know he is working towards that end. However, I do not know whether it is fully realized just how urgent the need is for something to be done in the very near future in that regard. I would hope that the park would be labelled as a natural playground as much as possible and yet have the facilities for. through traffic developed through this area within the very near future.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's statement as given on July 12 and completed this afternoon. I agreed with his attitude towards our national parks so much that I had great difficulty in not saying "amen" a good many times. However, one must realize that the minister does not make a comprehensive and complete statement without a background of some fairly good officials. I want to pay a compliment to the officials of his department. I think we in Canada are very fortunate in having the officials we have in the water resources branch, the parks division, the forest branch, the wildlife service and the northern administration. In this department we have some officials whom I know other governments would be very pleased to take from us. I do not say that only from my personal experience. This is a particularly interesting department to me. I meet persons in universities and persons in other governments and I have heard those comments made on a number of occasions.
The minister has responsibility for a most interesting and important department. In fact, the welfare of millions of Canadians and their happiness to a great extent depend upon the policies and the administration of the minister's department. I have a few

Supply-Northern Affairs brief comments to make on particular items of the minister's estimates but at this time I want to advance what I consider to be a good idea. I must admit that those who know me say that I am rather fertile as far as ideas are concerned. Once upon a time I thought I had invented a device for perpetual motion but it did not work. However, I invented an everlasting stoneboat that would nearly run itself. I have experimented with so many things in my lifetime that my wife and daughters are now inclined to refer to me as Major Hoople. Anyway, I suggest that the idea 1 wish to advance briefly this evening is a sound and good idea.
For several years I have introduced a resolution urging a federal-provincial conference on conservation with a view to establishing a nation-wide policy on this question. However, at this time I wish to stress the necessity for a national voluntary organization that would promote an understanding, as a result of voluntary action, of the principles of conservation and would develop what I think should be termed an ecological conscience in Canada.
We in this group are concerned with the health of human beings and the health of our national resources. I think that fact has been very appropriately indicated this evening by the remarks of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort who does not think it worth while to stop and listen to what I am going to say this evening. He dealt with the human resources that come under the administration of the minister's department. I am going to deal very briefly with the renewable natural resources. I think that on the health of both of those resources depends the prosperity and the happiness of the Canadian people.
I suggest that this department and the provincial departments of a similar nature require the co-operation of a national voluntary organization to assist them in the same way as the Health League of Canada assists the Department of National Health and Welfare and the provincial health departments.
I understand that the Health League of Canada was formed in 1921, at the request of this dominion government, to assist in a nation-wide publicity program and campaign in connection with the co-operative efforts of the dominion and provincial governments to control certain diseases at that time. In view of the need for popular education in many health fields, the scope of this organization has greatly broadened in recent years, and it now undertakes a nation-wide education program in the field of health generally. It also sponsors two annual events in Canada,
[Mr. Herridge.l
namely national health week and national immunization week which I understand are considered to be the greatest single annual events of this type recognized in Canada. These events receive the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments. I understand that the health league also publishes a national magazine known as "Health" and sends weekly news releases on health to all the newspapers in Canada in French and in English. In recognition of the valuable services it renders in this field-services that a government department cannot render, namely in education and the building up of public opinion in support of progressive health legislation-the government of Canada in recent years has been in the habit of giving a grant of $10,000 a year. I think that is far too little. As a matter of fact, had I been in the committee the other day when these estimates were under consideration, I intended to say so. But you cannot be in two places at once. I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that we need a similar type of national voluntary organization to perform similar services in preserving the health of our national resources in this country. I believe we need two aspects of co-operation. We need government organization, government conferences decisions and programs. If these are going to be promoted and administered effectively, we need the same type of voluntary organization in this field that we have in the field of national health and welfare. I know that in this country at the present time we have the Canadian Forestry Association, the Agricultural Institute of Canada and various engineering institutes and wildlife organizations all doing valuable work in their particular fields. However, while they all do a certain amount of educational and publicity work, their problems are largely technical and scientific. The greater part of their membership is composed of men with technical training and experience in the development of research and programs and things of that type.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we need a national voluntary organization to supplement the activities of government. Such an organization, in my opinion, could deal with the subject in general, not in a scientific way, in order to build up a philosophy in support of the spirit of conservation and it would obtain the support of multitudes in this country. Its prime purpose would be to get the people interested in and concerned about the conservation of our natural resources. Now, before proceeding-I am not going to detain the house very long this evening-I do want to quote very briefly from an excellent article that came into my hands. This was an address, I believe, given by Mr. Mair, who is

director of the wildlife service, to a wildlife conference in the United States. It is entitled "Towards an ecological conscience". I do consider that an excellent title. I would advise anyone who is interested in this subject to get a copy of this address. I think in its general contribution to the whole question it is well worth anyone's while studying and publicizing the ideas contained therein.
I just want to quote two or three brief paragraphs because I think Mr. Mair has presented the subject in a most interesting and, in my opinion, somewhat unusual manner. He has this to say in one place:
Let us confine our thinking for the moment, however, to the more immediate future. There is grave reason to doubt that we are presently sufficiently aware of our own place in the web of life to intelligently utilize our natural resources. To quote from another article, published in the Pennsylvania Game News: ". . . We have never learned the art of living with each other in this world without destroying ourselves and the natural resources that have made possible this great technological progress. Our tendency towards wars of self-destruction is surpassed only by our devastation of the resources that support them."
Then, there are two more paragraphs which I think are well worth inserting in the record.
Those of us convinced of the vital place of nature, its waters, trees, flowers and wildlife, in our way of life must be strong to fight for retention of adequate living space for all these and ourselves today, and every day. But we must do very much more. We must be unceasing in our efforts to bring to others an understanding and an appreciation of the ecological concept and their place in it, of the land ethic and their close dependence upon soil and water.
Then, again:
We must ensure that our people become Intellectually and emotionally concerned with the land and water and the complex pattern of growth they support. Unless we can do this, to the end that every person, from the trapper and farmer to the business magnate and legislator, is proud to work with our living natural resources rather than ready to abuse them, we are fighting a losing battle.
I think Mr. Mair puts the ecological concept of the problem before us in very interesting language. I think if that is going to be done we have to have more than just government action. We have to have voluntary action along very much the same lines as we have voluntary action in support of the Department of National Health and Welfare. We have the foundation for such an organization now. We have the various conservation leagues in the various provinces across Canada. We have the wildlife associations:	we have
naturalists societies and we have youth organizations that could be utilized to great advantage. In British Columbia we have an annual provincial conference on natural resources. What we need is co-ordination of all these voluntary activities on a national 67509-439
Supply-Northern Affairs basis to focus attention on this question, to develop interest and carry on a continual educational program.
This will require three or four things. It will require naturally a small, devoted and well informed national staff. It would demand an annual conference something after the fashion of the conference held in the United States by the wildlife organization, which over there also includes forestry resources, water resources and so on. It will require a national magazine of popular content, not a technical magazine. It will require continual publicity, news releases in the press after the fashion of the national health league. Now, if we can get this type of organization going by co-ordinating all the persons and organizations interested in this country, I think we can do a great deal. The work ought to be supported by much greater expenditures on the part of federal and provincial governments in the protection of these most valuable natural resources.
Now, all this will require money. In my opinion the minister's department would be well advised to copy the example set by the dominion government in 1921 when it invited the public to form a national organization on a voluntary basis and at that time gave a grant of $20,000 a year. I think the minister's department would be well advised if it were to promote the same type of national organization that would have a popular appeal and that would build up support for this idea across the country, and I suggest do the same work for the health of our natural resources as the health league is doing for the health of human beings. Now, such an organization, if it were developed and promoted, should receive grants from the federal government and possibly some assistance from the provincial governments.
There is one point I wish to make. We have a lot of Canadians who have benefited materially and financially from the development and exploitation of natural resources. I think the support for such an organization provides a splendid opportunity for our wealthier citizens to assist in financing this type of educational organization. I believe this is a very necessary step in the development of the concept of an over-all conservation program across this country. In my opinion, we must use every effort possible to bring Canadians to an appreciation of their kinship with the soil and the resources which sustain and develop the abundant life which we in Canada at this time are fortunate to enjoy. I believe this can be done most effectively by the co-operation of the government and a voluntary organization such as I have suggested. When the minister replies on the various items I would very much like-I have

Supply-Northern Affairs submitted my resolution for quite a number of years without much success-to hear his comments on the suggestion I have put forward at this time.

speechtext:
The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources covers a great variety of activities. I do not intend at this time, and at this late hour in our proceedings to make any comprehensive or detailed survey. Rather, I would reserve any comments I have to make on the incidental items of the department until such time as we come to those items. Also, I would think it would be a good thing, if there are no other speakers, if we had a chance to hear a reply from the minister.
There is a matter that is in abeyance that I should like to bring once again to the attention of the house. I did so on June 22 and at that time the Minister of Finance, speaking for the government, said that a reply would be made at the appropriate time. I raise the matter again on the estimates of this department because it is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that this matter now lies, according to the information I have. I refer to the Fontana case, which is becoming somewhat of a celebrated case in Canada. It concerns the expropriation of a certain parcel of property in the vicinity of the town of Virden in the province of Manitoba. Just to give the committee and the minister some idea of the nature of this particular case I will take a few moments to review it briefly.
The case is named after one August Fontana who was farming this parcel of land up until the year 1940. At that time a part of his farm was required for use as an airport and expropriation action was taken by the government through a representative of the Canadian National Railways land branch to carry out the necessary proceedings with Mr. Fontana. Mr. Fontana, incidentally, was a successful farmer by this time, after having passed through difficult years of the early 1930's, the dirty thirties of the drought, and was once again on his feet in cultivating this land. He had come to this country from Italy in the early part of the century, and became a naturalized citizen in the year 1904. Since he was a patriotic Canadian, as I indicated on June 22, he quite willingly allowed his land to be used for defence purposes. Unfortunately, Mr. Fontana is not literate in the English language, and he was not fully aware of all the legal niceties involved in the expropriation transaction. Therefore, no steps were taken to reserve the mineral rights, although at that time-and I
[Mr. Herridge.l
feel this is important to the case-he did request the privilege of continuing to remove gravel from this particular piece of property. Since that time-in 1950 to be precise- minerals in this particular section of the country had become valuable. Oil had been discovered, and Mr. Fontana took steps to inquire about the ownership of the mineral rights. He was under the impression that they had been reserved in his name, but he discovered that they had been reserved by the crown and through a series of proceedings the crown refused to take any action to reconvey them or to make any compensation for their loss. The original price that was paid to Mr. Fontana was $9,000. When the minerals were offered for lease by the crown I believe a bid of some $200,000 was received, with other concessions. Therefore, it would appear that the crown stands to make a substantial sum of money at the expense of Mr. Fontana.
Various parties have concerned themselves with this particular case. I had a return on the subject brought down in the house on June 25 of this year. It is sessional paper No. 243. It contained many interesting letters from various people, legal advisers and so forth, who were making representations to the government on behalf of Mr. Fontana. One letter I do wish to refer to is from Dr. Hannam, who is president of the Canadian federation of agriculture. On March 15, 1955 he wrote to the Minister of Agriculture, and the two pertinent paragraphs I should like to place on the record are the following:
Considering that the action taken by Mr. Fontana in selling his land was involuntary in the first place, and that federal acquisition of the mineral rights was not necessary to the purpose for which the land was expropriated, it would not seem unreasonable to us that these mineral rights should revert to their original owner.
However, we understand the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, which has administration of these oil rights, as in an advanced stage of negotiations for selling them on lease, and court action to halt these negotiations has, as of today, failed. Mr. Gerrand is asking Mr. Lesage if he will hold up the completion of sale of the lease until he can, if his request is granted, make further representations on this matter to a committee of the cabinet. You have, we understand, a copy of the letter to Mr. Lesage. We certainly feel that Mr. Fontana's claim to consideration is sufficiently well-founded that completion of the lease arrangements should be held up until further consideration is given the possibility of returning the mineral rights on the property to him.
In the hope you will do whatever you can to avoid an injustice being done in this case, I am
Yours sincerely,
H. H. Hannam,
President and Managing Director.
A copy of the letter was sent to the Minister of Justice as well. Now, I re-echo the

sentiments of Dr. Hannam in reference to this case when he says that unless some action is taken to compensate Mr. Fontana for the inadvertent loss of what would have normally been his had he not been asked to surrender the property, unless something is done to recompense him, to make some suitable adjustment, it seems to me that a grave injustice is going to be done to this Canadian citizen. He is 88 years of age today; he has a large family who are also interested in the matter and, as I emphasized on June 22, he is merely asking for the same privileges that have arisen from the possession of this land in this particular section by other farmers who, because of fortuitous circumstances, were not required to surrender their parcels of property for defence purposes.
Several prominent lawyers have interested themselves in this case. Dr. Hannam, of the federation of agriculture, as I have already indicated, has become extremely interested and I feel it is important because it concerns the rights of a private citizen being invaded by government. I am sure that if the government will view it in this way they will take every step possible. Certainly, there are all sorts of provisions in the Expropriation Act to make it possible for them to compensate Mr. Fontana or reconvey the mineral rights to him. In this day and age when governments more and more are invading the rights of private property owners I think we should lean over backwards to see that no injustice is done to this particular citizen. I leave the matter with the minister; I believe it is the responsibility of his department.

Mr. Chairman, I raised this particular matter when the minister was introducing his bill concerning northern power development and I discovered I was somewhat out of order in doing so during the discussion on that particular piece of 67509-439J
Supply-Northern Affairs legislation. It would seem to me that item 293 concerning itself with the Northern Research Co-ordination Centre might have something to do with all manner of research that is taking place in northern Canada as well as the northern part of the U.S.S.R.
The minister will recall that the other day I referred to an article in the Financial Post of March 3, 1956 which suggested that rather interesting experiments were being carried out in weather modification and water diversion in the Soviet Arctic which would have some considerable bearing upon climatic conditions in Canada's northland.
In order to indicate that this is a subject which is being seriously considered I want to read a brief excerpt from this article which is entitled, "How Russ Plan to Heat Arctic Hits Canada". The author, a Mr. W. G. R. Cameron, is a responsible scientist, so I am told, and as the introduction to the article says:
This is not science fiction.
The article continues:
W. G. R. Cameron, the co-author of this article with Post staff writer Donald R. Gordon, is an eccnomist who has devoted special study to announced Russian plans to change the northern hemisphere. This article is based on Russian announcements and on the interpretation thereof by Canadian scientists.
Apparently our Canadian scientists are concerning themselves with this question. The body of the article goes on to say that as a result of the program that is to be undertaken by Russia we can perhaps anticipate:
A vast market garden in the Northwest Territories. Tennis in November on the shores of lake Athabaska.
The article goes on to state further:
. . . it's Russia's dream, and the dream could have that impact on Canada. As successive steps of the red master plan are completed, these disturbances could occur:
Disruption of the fragile climatic balance over Europe bringing longer, more bitter winter weather, eating into the vital European food growing season.
Diversion of chill Arctic waters down the Canadian east coast past Halifax, adding to storms and early frosts in the fall, lengthening the winter perhaps tying up Halifax as a winter port.
An estimated five foot rise in the world's ocean levels, flooding parts of London, New York, the Netherlands and hundreds of acres of coastal land.

I do not know who is going to make the decision but as I am on my feet, may I proceed? I understand we are on item 294 concerning national parks.
Some years ago I had occasion to quarrel with the administration of the national park at Waskesiu on the subject of what are commonly called shack tents. Might I say first of all that my main interest in Waskesiu as a national park is that it provides a healthful and pleasant holiday ground for many people who cannot afford to go elsewhere. I might say, too, that while it is outside of my constituency my particular concern is
[Mr. Dinsdale.)
due to the fact that the people of my city use that park almost exclusively as a holiday ground.
The shack tenter is usually a humble person. Quite often he does not have a car of his own and he has to use the facilities of bus transportation to go for his holiday.
I can well understand that it is a laudible ambition for the superintendent of a national park to keep the most frequented part in an orderly condition. He likes to have cottages built there that are a credit to the place; but if my conception of what a national park ought to be is correct, then I think there is some validity in my argument that these people should perhaps have even particular consideration.
The man who can afford a better holiday who is not pleased with the place can take his car and go off somewhere else and can afford to pay for accommodation. These people, however, are pretty well required to stay where they are because of their financial situation.
On the occasion I referred to a number of years ago, seven or eight years ago perhaps, these shack tenters had a very good location and were on the edge of the water. At that time the administration apparently thought of these shack tents as rather unsightly dwelling places and attempted to move them back into the bush away from the best facilities. They rented and sold the ground previously occupied by the shack tenters at expensive rates to people who could construct a class of cottage that was acceptable in the eyes of the park administration. I did take up the matter with the department. I think I had some influence in getting a better deal for those people, because, particularly in a national park, I think, those people have just as much right as anyone else to the waterfront. That went along for two or three years, but after that they were not able to resist the pressure and they were moved away from there, with the result that the location is not as good as many other locations were. That is the background.
Now I want to come to the particular situation today and I want to put in a particular plea with the minister for the type of person to make sure that those people have at least equal consideration with other people, and when they have set up homesteads-I use that word, of course, in a metaphorical sense -when they have squatted, if you like, or homesteaded on that particular piece of ground, I think it would have to be something important before they are moved away from a place which they have used for years. I expect that the same applies not only to the national park at Waskesiu but to other national parks of the same nature.

Now I come to my second point, and it is very short, that is to say, a great many of these people who build shack tents think that there is a good deal of unnecessary fuss about having to take them down every year. Whether they use this piece of land with the shack tent on it for one month or for two or three, they are charged the same fee, and under those circumstances they think they should be allowed to leave that building, because it is a little building, in position. Some of them think they should not be forced to take these things down in the wintertime. Although they are only going to spend a week or two weeks there, they have to have that erected again, and they are put to a considerable amount of trouble.
Just for the record, I want to define what I mean by a shack tent. A shack tent is a small building of which the walls are made of lumber, and it is customary to have on top, to cast off the rain, a peaked roof usually made of canvas. Those who complain about this say that most of them would be perfectly willing, if the department would allow them, to leave those things there permanently and that they would be perfectly willing to finish them off in a more substantial shape by putting on a permanent roof rather than the wobbly canvas thing, which gets out of repair and makes the place look not as neat as it otherwise would be. That is a cause for complaint, and, although it is not my constituency, I make no apologies for raising the point, because it is the people of Saskatoon city in particular, and more than other people, who use that as a playground.
However, the regulation of the department as it is now, I understand, is that these things have to be taken down. The top has to be removed. The sides have to be piled up. I presume that a caretaker or someone at the park takes care of them. When these people come up for a short holiday for a few weeks in the following summer, the whole process has to be gone through again and the thing has to be erected, only to be taken down in the immediate future.
Those are the two points I wanted to draw to the minister's attention. If I have to make a judgment, the first one is the more important, that is to say, a rather humble person who probably needs a holiday more than the others but who cannot be selective in a choice of a location or indeed of a park should get some special consideration in that matter, particularly if he has established through time something of a right in that particular manner. I should like to hear from the minister, who has his officials in front of him, his comment on what I have said and whether
Supply-Northern Affairs he could tell me if in fact I have painted something of a true picture of the situation.

The plea that has been made by the hon. member for Saskatoon is exactly the kind of demand that I deplored this afternoon when I outlined what the policy of the department was on the national parks. The shack tents in Waskesiu are not very beautiful to see. I do not know whether the hon. member for Saskatoon has seen them as I have seen them, but they are certainly not a great asset to the beauty of the national parks. It is not surprising that we have to have certain regulations.
This afternoon when I was outlining the policy that we should follow with regard to the parks, one which was approved tonight by the hon. member for Kootenay West, a colleague of the hon. member for Saskatoon, I said:
When It becomes necessary, in view of the greatly increased numbers of visitors, to rearrange camp grounds or to restrict their use to the period of a normal holiday, and when in the course of these changes certain persons lose some of the privileges they have enjoyed in the past, such as that of occupying the best place in the camp grounds over a whole season,-
And I could add "season after season."
-we are told that we are depriving people of their rights, and our decisions can be most unpopular among the groups concerned.
That is what I said this afternoon, and I added:
We do our best to meet particular interests when this can be done without prejudice to all the people of Canada; but once a situation becomes such that the interest of the people as a whole is suffering or is likely to suffer in future, we are duty bound to all Canadians-to whom the parks belong-to make the best rearrangements we can make.
I went to Waskesiu and I saw the shack tents. I know the condition of the people who use them, and I do not want to deprive those people of the only vacation they can get that is within their means, as the hon. member for Saskatoon has said, and I agree with him on that. However, they must understand that when they go to the parks they are not going to a summer vacation home that they have bought, on land that they own. They are going to a park which belongs to the whole people of Canada, and it is not the man who wants to stay in Waskesiu because he lives in Saskatoon and it is easy for him to go to Waskesiu. It is not his particular interest that should be the determining factor in our policy towards the park. It is in the interests of all the people of Canada that the natural beauty of this park be conserved as much as possible in its natural beauty for the whole of the people of Canada. That is our policy.

Supply-Northern Affairs

My point is that the question of enjoyment has been sacrificed to a foolish idea of what the minister considers beauty. The minister says that the natural beauty of any park must be preserved. No one can agree with him more than I do, but I am going to suggest that the way to preserve the natural beauty of a woods and lake park is

not to build town houses in it with beer stores and all the rest of the silly things that we have to put up with around our homes. When we go to this place we find city conditions, exactly the same conditions that prevail in the cities, and the people who can least afford that sort of thing are shoved back into the woods.
I am not going to use the word "slums" but according to the minister's ideas apparently that is what he will be prepared to create. You will be prepared to create an aristocracy in the place close to the water with the best conditions and all the rest of it and, somewhere in the bush behind, you are going to put the people who do not matter too much. I am warming up a little on the subject, and may I say that this is not the only direction in which this government shows the same kind of preference for this kind of people and not for the others. Mr. Chairman, I have some remarks I want to make on item 294. I happen to be here now and if we are going to continue consideration of the minister's estimates in committee I cannot really see any reason why I should not go on. I do not want to interrupt the orderly procedure of the committee, but I came here from one of the standing committees hoping that I might have a chance to say a few words on this item. I do not want to extend the sitting tonight beyond the wishes of other hon. members, but I cannot see that we will make much more headway by doing one thing than by doing another.
As it happens, the subject matter on which I want to say a few words is related to the remarks just made by the hon. member for New Westminster. In considering the item having to do with the administration of national historic sites at this session I feel that something should be said about the forthcoming centennial celebration in the province of British Columbia. I hope that the centennial, about which something has already been said in connection with the minting of a special coin, will be an event which will enable members of the house from other parts of Canada and the people of Canada generally to come to realize that when British Columbia entered confederation it did so as a crown colony which already had something of a history behind it.
I have noticed that there is some little disposition on the part of the people in the eastern parts of Canada to fail to realize that fact. I think there is a tendency to regard British Columbia as an adjunct to upper and lower Canada which suddenly came into being because of confederation. I hope that a growing sense of appreciation of the history and traditions of British Columbia will arise out of the centennial. Not long ago it happened to come to my notice, and I was a little startled by it, that the historic city of Halifax which, if my date is correct, was founded in the year 1746-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
1749-is only 100 years older than the city of Victoria which some people may regard as being out in the raw, wild and woolly west. I think it is important to realize, that without British Columbia in being as a crown colony at the time of confederation, Canada as we know it today would probably not exist because there would not have been a western anchor to tie Canada together.
Supply-Northern Affairs I think it is also important to realize something of how that came to happen. Along with the member for New Westminster I also am very glad that historic Fort Langley is going to be restored. However, I should like to point out that Fort Langley and New Westminster are in fact by-products rather than the cause of the coming into being of British Columbia. They came into being because of the discovery of gold. If we are going to give recognition to what caused British Columbia to come into being to create the anchor which made Canada as a nation extending ocean to ocean possible, we must cast our minds into a rather plain and ordinary little gash between two hills in the heartland of the Cariboo in British Columbia and recognize that while, at a casual glance that little strip of land there is like a thousand and one other places in Canada, nevertheless, because in that valley there was discovered the richest piece of placer ground of its size that has ever been found anywhere on the face of the earth, British Columbia came into being as we know it today; that it became something more than a fur-trading outpost, which I think in all probability would have fallen into the hands of the expanding United States. For that reason, and because I happen to have lived for a number of years in that particular little area, and perhaps caught something of the spirit of the pioneers of British Columbia that I feel one can still hear whispering in the quiet hills of the Cariboo, I should like to suggest that, in this centennial celebration, and perhaps in some renewed interested on the part of the national historic sites and monuments people, the historic site of Barkerville will not be forgotten. I do not think that the matter of some suitable recognition and restoration of Barkerville would be as expensive as that of the restoration of Fort Langley. But nevertheless because of the fact that Barkerville came into being, I think I would venture to say that Canada as we know it today exists, and has its being as a national entity. I am very happy to know, in making particular mention of Barkerville tonight, that His Excellency the Governor General did see fit in his recent tour of British Columbia to make a special side trip from Quesnel back into the hinterland 60 miles to Barkerville, and that while he was there he met some of the oldtimers there, including that grand old man named Fred Tregillus, whom it would be a privilege for anybody to know. I hope the report which His Excellency will bring back with him of his tour of British Columbia will perhaps help to emphasize what I myself feel about Barkerville as a valuable historic site in Canada.

Supply-Northern Affairs
Barkerville was in its heydays in the early 1860's. Because of the fact that the entire town was burned in the winter of 1868-69, nothing really exists there which antedates the rebuilding in 1869. Some very interesting buildings were built by the people, many of them young sons of the province of Ontario who lie buried in the old graveyard there. Unfortunately many of those original buildings have gone which were there when I first saw the town. I think for example of the old Royal Cariboo Hospital building, of the No. 2 Masonic Lodge building of British Columbia, and of the old Theatre Royal which have all gone. In the days when Barkerville was the second largest place west of Chicago on this North American continent, stock companies used to travel all the way from San Francisco to play the Theatre Royal in Barkerville. You can imagine what a trip that must have been in those days.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: They had a brewery, too.

Oh, yes. I myself have seen the remnants of some of the old stage settings that used to be used in the Theatre Royal in those days. I do not know whether or not any of those are left around Barkerville. I could tell at some length some of the things that I learned from some of the early pioneers who were still living while I was there, but I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee tonight. However, I want to point out that in addition to the rather historic church which was built in 1869 there is still in existence one other building which I feel is worthy of preservation as a national monument in Canada. I refer to the old court house at Richfield which lies just above the present site of Barkerville. I paid a visit to that building last summer on my way home from the session. I must say that I was grieved to see this building slowly but surely destroyed as something of permanent value, although a number of years ago some work was done on that building by the British Columbia historical society in putting in new foundations. This is the court house where the first chief justice of British Columbia, namely the famous Chief Justice Begbey, held court. That is a building which I feel should be preserved. It is true that there is one of those stone cairns at the entrance to Barkerville marking the end of the Cariboo trail. But apart from that, very little indication of national interest in that site has occurred. I hope that, in co-operation with the interested people and agencies in British Columbia, during the period approaching the centennial year the national historical sites and monuments people and the minister will 

take some special interest in the retaining of Barkerville as one of the most historic and significant national sites which has gone to the making of Canada as we have it today.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Just a brief word, Mr. Chairman; I would be remiss in my duty if I did not make an annual report on the progress of the international peace garden. The grant for the international peace garden is $10,000, and I suppose the argument that was raised by the hon. member for Calgary North with reference to the grant in aid of the Jack Miner foundation would also apply to the international peace garden; in fact, it would apply to a greater extent because unfortunately recently, owing to a misunderstanding of the importance of this very worth-while project, the grant was discontinued for a short period and then restored at the reduced rate of $10,000. I say "reduced rate" because for several years the international peace garden was supported to the extent of $15,000 a year. Rather than meeting the problem of the inflationary conditions by an increase in the grant, it has been decreased.
I draw this matter to the attention of the minister because I am sure that, as a result of all the representations that have been made in recent years by members of the cabinet and by citizens across the country, he is fully aware of the importance of this development not only as a symbol of the universal longing for peace but also as a practical tourist attraction. The tourist industry in Canada has been lagging in recent years in comparison with the relative number
of Canadians visiting the United States. But, so far as the peace garden is concerned, the reverse is true, there is a larger number making a pilgrimage to this very important development. For example, last year cars from 48 states were registered in the garden. There were international visitors from countries as far away as Scotland, Switzerland, South India, South Rhodesia, and so on. More and more voluntary groups having an interest in international affairs are choosing this site for their gatherings. For example, an international band camp was held. Some of the outstanding musicians of this continent were brought in.
I do not need to enlarge further on the theme, Mr. Chairman, except to point out that this is a very worth-while development. I do hope that the government can see its way clear at least to restoring the grant to the former level. The development on the United States side of the boundary is moving ahead much more rapidly than on the Canadian side, and I am sure, in the interest of national prestige, national pride, almost everyone would like to see us keep up our end of this development.
